articles.headline: Yaxel Lendeborg gave away $9m in NIL to give Steph Curry hope and join Wilt Chamberlain in NBA history
keyFacts: Golden State Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg scored 37 points to lead his team to a 124-112 win over the Los Angeles Clippers.
Warriors head coach Steve Kerr praised Lendeborg, stating that the rookie is highly skilled and still learning the NBA game.
Lendeborg joined Wilt Chamberlain and Rick Barry as the only Warriors in team history to average at least 20 points through seven games.
body: Yaxel Lendeborg is an ‘old’ NBA rookie who challenged the Golden State Warriors as soon as he was drafted.
Eight games into his pro career, Lendeborg is giving Stephen Curry new hope and has already seen his 24-year-old name mentioned next to NBA legend Wilt Chamberlain.
Yaxel Lendeborg has already written his name into Golden State history getty

“Whenever Steph’s not in the game, it’s my opportunity to try to be the leader, be the main guy on the team,” said Lendeborg, after scoring a personal best 37 points and lifting the Curry-less Warriors to a 124-112 win over the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday.
Two days later, Lendeborg scored 16 points and helped Golden State overcome the ejection of Draymond Green in a 116–113 win over Dillon Brooks and the Phoenix Suns .
“He’s playing this way and he really doesn’t know the NBA game yet,” Warriors head coach Steve Kerr said .
“The game is still really fast for him, but he’s so skilled and so talented that he’s making all kinds of plays. He’s going to get a lot better.”
Kerr has regularly praised Lendeborg, while the Warriors (5-3) have answered an 0-3 start by regularly relying on the No. 11 overall pick of the recent NBA Draft.
Lendeborg can be unfiltered in interviews and isn’t afraid to battle against the biggest basketball names in the world.
“I had a lot of respect for him (Luka Doncic because) I didn’t really watch the NBA much,” Lendeborg said two weeks ago.
“I just watched highlights and seen him kill people. But being in it firsthand and seeing all the whining and complaining, I lost all respect.”

To reach The Association, the 6-foot-9 and 247lb forward bounced from little known Arizona Western College and UAB to Michigan, where he won the 2025-26 NCAA championship under then-Wolverines coach Dusty May.
Lendeborg was born on September 30,2022 in San Juan, Puerto Rico and attended high school in Pennsauken, New Jersey.
Lendeborg has become a new face for the Warriors who can help Stephen Curry getty
Lendeborg traveled an unconventional route to reach the NBA getty
Curry finally has scoring help after watching Klay Thompson leave Getty
Known to some fans as the ‘Dominican LeBron,’ the Warriors rookie forward could have gone pro in 2025.
But he turned down $9 million in NIL money from Kentucky, eventually receiving $5m from Michigan to remain a Wolverine.
The Warriors then made the former junior college athlete the No. 11 pick in a 2026 NBA Draft that featured AJ Dybantsa , Darryn Peterson and Cam Boozer at the top.
Boozer is currently the betting favorite to win the 2026-27 NBA Rookie of the Year but Lendeborg’s stock is surging.
He’s averaging 21.5 points, 7 rebounds and 3.9 assists while shooting 50 percent from the field, and has surprised the Warriors by shooting 40 percent on 3-pointers.
After scoring 37 points against the Clippers, Curry’s new teammate joined Rick Barry and Chamberlain as the only Warriors in team history to average at least 20 points through seven games.
“It’s remarkable the impact he’s making on these games in the first couple weeks of the season,” Kerr said. “It changes everything.”

articles.headline: McTominay returns as Penrice earns first Scotland call
keyFacts: Scott McTominay, Kieran Tierney, and Che Adams return to the Scotland squad for upcoming Nations League matches after previous absences due to medical issues.
Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli selected a 26-player squad that features a first-ever call-up for left-back James Penrice.
Scotland sits third in Group B1 and needs at least four points in their remaining matches against North Macedonia and Switzerland to reach the promotion play-offs.
body: Scott McTominay missed games for club and country in September and October following a minor heart procedure [Getty Images] Scott McTominay, Kieran Tierney and Che Adams return to the Scotland squad for the remaining Nations League matches at home to North Macedonia and away to Switzerland.
There is a first call up for James Penrice and uncapped Kristi Montgomery, a late addition last time, retains his place.
Scott McKenna and Kenny McLean miss out through injury, while Lennon Miller, Josh Doig, Colby Donovan and James Wilson drop out.
Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli chose an extended pool of 28 for the first four matches, which included disappointing home defeats to Switzerland and Slovenia.
For these fixtures, the Belgian has gone with 26, sticking with four goalkeepers.
Scotland are third in Group B1 and require a minimum of four points to have any chance of finishing second to feature in the promotion play-offs.
One point would stave off any threat of relegation.
Switzerland lead the way on maximum points, with Slovenia three ahead of Scotland.
Left-back Penrice, 27, has impressed with Rangers since arriving on loan from AEK Athens, while Blackburn Rovers midfielder Montgomery, 22, has started all but one Championship match this season.
Napoli star McTominay has scored four goals in seven outings since recovering from a minor heart procedure.
Adams has doubled his Torino tally for the term with two goals in five Serie A games after a brief lay off with an adductor issue.
Captain Andy Robertson will surpass Sir Kenny Dalglish's record of 102 caps should the Tottenham full-back feature in both matches.

articles.headline: "There’s always a night when Rome burns": South Of Midnight director says that Xbox funding it was "unsustainable", at least in hindsight
keyFacts: Compulsion Games parted ways with Xbox during mass cuts, according to the article.
South of Midnight creative director David Sears said Xbox funding the game was unsustainable in hindsight.
Compulsion Games now owns the rights to their games and is looking for co-development work.
body: Compulsion Games parted ways with former owners Xbox, having landed on the long list of things Microsoft were determined to ditch as part of multi-round mass cuts this year. Now, South of Midnight creative director David Sears has suggested that an eventual pulling of the rug was something he feared throughout the game's development, to the point where he seemingly doesn't think he'd have funded it if he'd been in the shoes of Xbox execs.

In an interview with MinnMax, Sears - who left Compulsion in March 2025 - outlined that ideally games big publishers put out aim to fall into one of two buckets. They either make lots of money or increase the prestige of the brand by becoming cultural touchstones across multiple generations. Obviously doing both is the perfect outcome, but Sears pegged South of Midnight as being more geared towards the latter camp. The likes of Double Fine's Keeper and Obsidian's Pentiment are other games which off the top of my head could be said to fit that same mold. The issue, of course, is that when push comes to shove, it's the games which can show a strong bottom line at any given moment which make the best case for their studios' short term survival if cash is tight.

So, South of Midnight lived in a risky place, with Sears recalling: "I literally told people. I was like, yeah, this could be terrible because somebody is going to say, one day, 'The money tap, we're closing those floodgates' and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream". The interviewer then asked Sears if what he was getting at is that, while he's glad Xbox funded South of Midnight, he might not have done so or at least cut the funding earlier if he was in charge of the console maker.

"Yeah, probably," Sears replied. "I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. I mean, it's easy to dissect it now, right? But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they] would be like, 'How is this happening? I mean, how did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now'. There's always a night when Rome burns and I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Notably, Sears added that in his view modern Microsoft showed a "more humane" side than the version of the company that existed in the 90s and early 2000s by giving studios like Compulsion a chance to spin out on their own rather than simply shuttering them outright once they were deemed surplus to requirements.

Given the director's no longer at Compulsion, it seems he'll not have a say on what their next game looks like, but as a newly indie studio one would imagine they'll have a keen eye on the bottom line.

articles.headline: WoW: Forever Makes Every Class More Powerful in Last-Minute Change
keyFacts: Blizzard increased damage output for every class and raised high-level creature health in a final patch before World of Warcraft: Forever launches.
Blizzard stated it will leave class balance unchanged until the first raids open on December 9, after which a tuning pass will occur.
World of Warcraft: Forever launches on November 4 or 5 with updated gamepad support and increased creature respawn rates for lower-level zones.
body: Blizzard has detailed a final round of fixes and balance changes that it's making to World of Warcraft: Forever, based on feedback from the recent beta, before the retro MMO launches this week. The headline change is both simple and pretty dramatic: every class will do more damage.

In patch notes published on the official WoW forums, the developers explained that they had realized that sticking to the original game's power budgets for each class "meant that every new element we added needed to come at the expense of something else. Those reductions left some iconic abilities feeling lackluster, and closed the door to other potentially exciting design options."

The solution, Blizzard has decided, is to raise damage across every class and increase the health of high-level creatures to compensate. "This additional 'headroom' has allowed us to tune things to a place that we hope feels better overall," the developers said.
Blizzard fine-tunes classes and more before WoW: Forever's launch

The patch notes also include a raft of tuning for a wide range of classes and specs, which Blizzard said was aimed at distinguishing Forever's changes to classic WoW from those made in early expansions The Burning Crusade and Wrath of the Lich King. "Our aim in class design is not perfect numerical equality, but rather for every class to feel valuable to the groups they join, with powerful, unforgettable moments brought on by mastering them," Blizzard said.

The developer said that it would now leave balance alone until Forever's raids open a month after launch, on Dec. 9. Then it will make a "large tuning pass" based on data gathered from the live game, including on players leveling past 30 (the level cap in the beta).

Other changes in the patch notes include increased creature respawn rates in lower-level zones, to support the "large player volumes" Blizzard expects at launch, and a huge update to WoW: Forever's official gamepad support, which Blizzard reckons has now "entered a complete functional state" in which "all major gameplay and core user interface experiences can be played with a controller."

World of Warcraft: Forever, a reimagined version of classic WoW as it was in 2004 with updates and new content, launches on Nov. 4 (or Nov. 5, depending on your time zone). If the beta is any indication, it's going to be extremely popular.

articles.headline: Upcoming Final Fantasy 14 update should massively cut down on dungeon queue times
keyFacts: Square Enix announced that same-region player matchmaking for Final Fantasy 14 will launch on November 10 following a successful trial in Japan.
The update aims to reduce long queue times for specific alliance raids and improve overall group organization across logical data centers.
Players will also be able to use party finders, cross-world linkshells, and friend list functionality within the same physical data center.
body: Final Fantasy 14's queues can get long—not for roulettes, mind, those are usually pretty nippy—but if you're trying to complete a specific alliance raid as a newer player, you can be stuck twiddling your thumbs for ages.

Square Enix is planning to make a change that'll fix that soon, though. In a recent blog post to the game's website, it's been announced that same-region player matchmaking'll be available starting November 10 after a successful trial period on its Japanese servers.

What does that mean? Basically, FF14's server architecture is into physical data centers (Japan, Europe, Oceania, and North America), then logical data centers, which are sort of like realms in other MMOs. For instance, the NA servers have Crystal, Aether, Dynamis, and Primal (then within those centers are "worlds", which can be travelled and matchmade between pretty easily).

You've been able to hop between these logical data centers manually for some time—it's pretty common, for instance, for Crystal players to hop on over to Aether to group up with folks for high-end content. But you need to log out to do so, with said parties constructed through the in-game party finder.

After November 10, however, matchmaking for things like roulettes will also be possible within the same physical data center, as will the party finder writ large, cross-world linkshells, fellowships, and friend list and /tell functionality. Travelling between data centers will also be made easier, too.

This is a huge quality-of-life boost that should massively cut down on queueing times—but it'll also make organising or creating groups for the aforementioned high-end content way easier, too, allowing folks to see and join listings for different logical data centers without having to hop between them.

My secret hope, as an EU player who's currently stuck on North American ping for community reasons (it's where all my mates are), is that this sort of functionality might one day lead to cross region travel so I can hop on over to the EU whenever I actually want to do content. A guy can dream.

Harvey's history with games started when he first begged his parents for a World of Warcraft subscription aged 12, though he's since been cursed with Final Fantasy 14-brain and a huge crush on G'raha Tia. He made his start as a freelancer, writing for websites like Techradar, The Escapist, Dicebreaker, The Gamer, Into the Spine—and of course, PC Gamer. He'll sink his teeth into anything that looks interesting, though he has a soft spot for RPGs, soulslikes, roguelikes, deckbuilders, MMOs, and weird indie titles. articles.headline: Who will govern Israel? It may come down to Arab voters.
keyFacts: Israeli left-wing activists hold placards and chant slogans during a demonstration calling for a formation of a government together with Arab parties in Tel Aviv on October 28, 2026, a day after Israel's legislative elections.

| Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images The dust is beginning to settle a week after Israel’s first national election since Hamas’s attack on October 7, 2023 , and the war Israel waged on Gaza in response.
Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his opponents won the 61 parliamentary seats needed to govern.
body: Israeli left-wing activists hold placards and chant slogans during a demonstration calling for a formation of a government together with Arab parties in Tel Aviv on October 28, 2026, a day after Israel's legislative elections. | Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images

The dust is beginning to settle a week after Israel’s first national election since Hamas’s attack on October 7, 2023 , and the war Israel waged on Gaza in response. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his opponents won the 61 parliamentary seats needed to govern.

Now the fate of the next government hinges on a less-discussed part of the Israeli electorate: Arab citizens , who voted in record numbers and whose parties have emerged with more leverage than ever before. They are not to be confused with the roughly 5.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, who live under Israeli control but are not citizens and cannot vote in national elections.

Although Israel has become a fault line in both American parties, with Democrats split over arms sales and whether to call the war in Gaza a genocide , and Republicans over whether Israel pulled the United States into war with Iran, these were not the central issues in the recent election.

Voters and candidates alike treated the election as a referendum on Netanyahu himself, who has governed Israel for most of the past 17 years and is currently on trial for corruption. And Netanyahu did lose support in this election: His right-wing and religious coalition fell from 64 of the Knesset’s 120 seats in 2022 to 53, while 67 seats went to parties that ran against him.

Nineteen of those 67 opposition seats were won by two Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, on a historic surge in turnout among Arab citizens of Israel. Arab parties had held just 10 seats after the last election.
Key takeaways
Israel’s election ended in deadlock, and record Arab turnout nearly doubled Arab parties’ seats to 19, the most ever.
A crime wave in Arab towns while Netanyahu’s far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir ran the police drove Arab voters to the polls.
Depending on the details, a Jewish-Arab coalition could reshape Israeli politics, but it won’t end the occupation or reverse course in Gaza.

But most of Israel’s Jewish parties have long treated a governing coalition that depends on Arab votes as taboo. Netanyahu spent the campaign portraying Ra’am and Joint List politicians as supporters of terrorism , and several of his Jewish opponents promised to never govern with them. Whether the four Jewish-led opposition parties that call themselves the “change bloc” will break that promise is now the central political question hanging over Israel — with major implications for Arab and Jewish citizens alike, and for what kind of country they share.

“There’s been a fair amount of commentary from American Jewish groups that over a million Arab citizens can vote, and that’s true, but the big asterisk is it matters only if those votes are taken seriously and if Arabs are treated as potential partners in a coalition,” Ilan Goldenberg, the chief policy officer for J Street, a liberal pro-Israel group founded as a counterweight to AIPAC, told me. “Otherwise it’s a pretty empty symbol, and it says something else about Israeli society and Israeli politics.”

Polling suggests most change bloc voters would accept a government that relied on Ra’am, if not the Joint List, whether inside the coalition or backing it from outside in exchange for policy commitments. Their leaders have been more cautious, though, partly because most Jewish Israelis still oppose an Arab-Jewish coalition and the politicians worry about losing those voters in the next election. Critics see that caution as the problem: Rather than try to bring the Israeli public along, the Jewish opposition leaders campaigned on rejecting an alliance they might need to form any kind of government at all.

It’s a pivotal moment for supporters of a liberal, democratic Israel, for those pushing sanctions and boycotts — some of whom want an end to Israel as a Jewish state — and for the roughly 900,000 Arab citizens who turned out to vote for urgent improvements in their daily lives. The next few months will decide who governs the country, whether Arab voters get real influence over policy or become further marginalized, whether pressure on Israel from abroad grows or fades, and whether anything changes for the Palestinians it rules.
Why Arab voters showed up

For Arab voters, this election was different in two ways. The Arab parties were more united than ever on a single priority — getting rid of Netanyahu — even if it meant working with Zionist parties whose vision of a Jewish state they’ve long opposed. And calls to boycott the vote, which Islamist and Palestinian nationalist groups within Israel’s Arab community have pushed in past elections on the grounds that voting legitimizes the state, were far more muted this time around.

The prime motivating factor for Arab voters was Netanyahu’s coalition itself, the most right-wing government in Israel’s history. Its national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was once convicted of inciting racism after displaying a sign reading “Expel the Arab enemy,” has overseen the police while organized crime has killed record numbers of Arab citizens. Homicides in Arab communities more than doubled between 2022 and 2025, and police solved just 12 percent of them in the first half of this year. Netanyahu’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who has said there is “no such thing as a Palestinian people,” also froze hundreds of millions of shekels promised to Arab towns, arguing the money would reach criminals. In 2025, Britain and four other countries sanctioned both men for inciting violence against Palestinians.

“The feeling is the state has completely failed to address criminal violence,” Yousef Munayyer, a Palestinian citizen of Israel and the head of the Palestine/Israel program at the Arab Center Washington DC , told me. “Brutal murders go uninvestigated and unsolved, and in many corners there’s a belief that the Israeli intelligence services are intentionally turning a blind eye.”

Hassan Jabareen, the executive director of Adalah , a legal advocacy group for Palestinian citizens of Israel, told me the Arab parties have been deliberately keeping their demands to things an anti-Netanyahu government could practically deliver, like fighting crime, ending the demolition of Bedouin homes in southern Israel, and stopping settler violence in the West Bank .

“We are not going to say to end the occupation, we are not going to ask for withdrawal from Syria,” Jabareen said. “Those issues, we know that they won’t agree with us, and the right-wing will use it against them, and they themselves won’t agree.”

Though Ra’am and the Joint List did not make Gaza central to their campaigns, Jabareen said the national election was a rare opportunity for Arab voters to express their anger at the war, something they’ve been heavily barred from protesting over the last three years. He added that Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank have been “happy and proud” of the record turnout of Arab citizens.
The choice facing Gadi Eisenkot

The “change bloc” is an alliance of four Zionist parties with little in common beyond wanting Netanyahu gone. Its leader is Gadi Eisenkot , a former army chief who sat in Netanyahu’s war cabinet after October 7, lost a son in Gaza, and quit the government over its handling of the war. His new centrist party won the most seats of the four. The others are a party led by two former prime ministers, the settler-right hawk Naftali Bennett and the centrist Yair Lapid, and Yair Golan’s party, the last of Israel’s Zionist left. The fourth is Avigdor Lieberman’s, hawkish on security and built on secular Russian-speaking immigrants who want the ultra-Orthodox out of government.

The four were split on Arab parties during the campaign. Golan was the only leader explicitly open to governing with them. Eisenkot set four conditions for any coalition partner, including recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state and Hamas as a terrorist group, and said in September that no Arab party met them. (Arab leaders and many critics saw these conditions as a way to shut Arabs out without saying so.) Bennett, who in 2021 led the first governing coalition ever to include an independent Arab party, said this time he wanted only Zionist parties in government, and Lieberman, who sat in that same 2021 coalition, also ruled out relying on Arab parties again.
Ori Kor, a progressive campaigner who worked for Golan’s left-wing party, told me most Jewish opposition voters “were shocked” on election night, expecting the change bloc to win more seats.

“What people really expected is that Netanyahu voters would not turn out as they did, because the logic was after three years of war, two failed wars against Iran, attacking Qatar, the sanctions, and the incredible physical, emotional and economic toll on the country every Israeli living here has experienced, that Netanyahu would pay some sort of cost,” he said. And while Netanyahu’s coalition did lose about a dozen seats compared to 2022, his party still did better than expected, beating the final polls from three major Israeli broadcasters.

So what is the resistance to forming a Jewish-Arab government? Part of it is plain prejudice, a refusal to accept Arab parties as legitimate partners in governing a Jewish state. Arab parties have supported or joined an Israeli government only twice, briefly, in the 1990s and in 2021, and both times the Jewish parties involved treated it as a one-off they’d rather not repeat. Both times, too, the Arab parties were just a handful of votes at the margin, while this time they would represent nearly a third of the coalition.

A vocal liberal minority of Israelis say that’s exactly the change the country is overdue for. In the week since the election, thousands have rallied to demand their leaders form a Jewish-Arab government. Some activists organized a pressure campaign outside Eisenkot’s home, while others have signed petitions, including one led by writers and artists , and another by Israeli healthcare professionals .

The other main hurdle, which can be hard to disentangle from bigotry, is electoral fear. Jewish opposition leaders worry that a Jewish-Arab coalition would be fragile from the start, and that if it collapsed in the near future, they would pay the price in the next election. Israelis vote on security above all, and Netanyahu leverages those concerns shamelessly. Two days before this past election, for example, he posted on X an AI-generated image of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv , warning of a second Holocaust if he lost. On election night he warned that it was “forbidden” to form a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties. (This didn’t stop Netanyahu himself from negotiating with Ra’am in 2021 , when he needed its votes.)

Ra’am, for its part, has spent the last few months trying to make itself an easier partner for Zionist parties to accept. In August its leader, Mansour Abbas, put a Jewish former deputy security minister in the No. 2 slot on the party’s electoral slate, and a few months earlier Ra’am cut its formal ties to the religious council that had guided its decisions, to show it answers to no one but its voters. Abbas has also repeatedly condemned the October 7 attack.

The Joint List is more nationalist, and one of its party leaders was forced out of the race in October over an article he published the day after October 7, calling the attack an “important historical event.” That leader has since said his language was badly worded and he did not mean support for it. The Joint List may not want to be formally in the coalition anyway. Its leaders have said they’d rather support an Eisenkot government from the outside, which would let them push for concessions on crime and budgets without having to share responsibility for the coalition’s decisions on Gaza and elsewhere.

For now, the Arab parties are signaling they don’t want to drive a hard bargain with Jewish leaders given the risk of Netanyahu staying in power. Over the weekend, one of the Joint List’s leaders said his party would back Eisenkot’s choice for Knesset speaker when the new parliament convenes on November 10. “We want to be part of the correction, part of the hope,” he said, adding that his party would “swallow frogs” to get things done. The Joint List’s chair also said the party was “truly ready” to help build a majority in the coming weeks. Opposition leaders have reportedly been in contact with both Joint List officials and Abbas.

Eisenkot, for his part, posted a statement over the weekend that read as tailored to exactly that arrangement, Ra’am inside and the Joint List outside. He repeated the four conditions he set during the campaign and wrote that “the door to the government we establish will be open to any elected official who accepts these principles.” But he also described the state he wants as “Jewish, democratic, liberal and egalitarian,” a word choice seemingly aimed at Arab citizens. And he said partners could satisfy his national-service condition through “civilian service,” not just the army, a voluntary version of which most Arab citizens tell pollsters they’d support.

The sticking point is Eisenkot’s demand that all partners declare Hamas a terrorist organization, something Abbas has repeatedly said he considers a risk to his life and his family’s. Hamas has a record of killing Palestinians accused of collaborating with Israel, and Abbas has faced death threats before.
But over the weekend Abbas signaled, according to Channel 12 , that Eisenkot’s conditions need not keep Ra’am out of a government, which suggests the two sides may be able to negotiate a compromise.
What a Jewish-Arab coalition means for Israel’s friends and critics

For supporters of a liberal, democratic Israel, bringing Arab parties into government would signal that Arab citizens have a say in who governs the country, and undercut the claim that they are shut out of power. Whether that proves true depends on what those parties actually get, in cabinet posts and in policy commitments.

Still, Israel’s democracy stops at the Green Line, the boundary that separated Israel from the West Bank before the 1967 war. More than 3 million Palestinians on the other side of it live under Israeli control with no vote in the government that rules them, and the same is true of the 2 million in Gaza. No election inside Israel changes that.

After last Tuesday’s election, most major American Jewish organizations released statements praising Israel’s democracy, citing its high turnout as proof. For example, AIPAC, which did not return requests for comment, praised turnout as reflecting Israel’s “vibrant democracy and rich diversity.” The Jewish Federations of North America cheered Israel for its “deep commitment to democratic principles and civic participation.”

J Street and New Jewish Narrative were exceptions, with J Street’s statement calling on the Jewish opposition to form a government with the Arab parties. New Jewish Narrative said Arab citizens “must be allowed a full voice in what comes next.”

Munayyer, of the Arab Center Washington DC, has little patience for the democracy talk at this moment. “People who are using this opportunity to talk about Israeli democracy, they’re not serious people,” he told me. Palestinian citizens did win historic numbers, but if the millions who live under Israeli control could actually vote, “they’d probably have 60 seats, not 19.” That, he said, is what makes it apartheid, noting South Africa held regular elections, too.

J Street’s Goldenberg was clear that a coalition with Arab parties would not by itself be a reason to ease pressure on Israel. The United States, he said, should decide what’s in its own national interest and respond when an Israeli government acts against it, whether on settler violence or on Gaza. But he argued that most Democrats have not given up on Israel. “I think the overwhelming majority of Democrats are not in a position of viewing Israel as irredeemable,” he told me. “What they want is a change in behavior.”

A government that depended on 19 Arab seats, he added, would be the clearest possible signal that there’s potential for change. “I can’t think of any single action the Israeli opposition could take that would buy Israel more goodwill,” Goldenberg said. “And I can’t think of anything that would further confirm for Democrats that this is not an Israel we can work with than a failure to try.”

Hadar Susskind, the president of New Jewish Narrative and a dual citizen who flew back to vote, doubted American Jews would have much influence over the forthcoming coalition talks. But if a new government forms, he told me, liberal Zionist groups like his see “a lot of positive opportunity” to work in both directions, pushing the new government to deliver real change and Congress to engage with it and hold it to account.

That possibility, a repaired relationship between Israel and the United States, is exactly what many of Israel’s staunchest critics are worried about. The Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement’s official statement on the election called Western attention to it a “desperate attempt” to rehabilitate Israel as a democracy and pin Gaza war crimes on Netanyahu alone. For BDS supporters and many other anti-Zionists, engaging with any Israeli government, however it’s composed, normalizes a state they deem illegitimate.

The journalist Mehdi Hasan, who runs the outlet Zeteo, made a narrower version of the same argument, saying his worry throughout the election has been that “political and media elites” will use it to push for a “reset” that could improve Israel’s standing in global public opinion. The push to condition military aid and sanction settlements gained ground around the world largely because of Netanyahu and his far-right ministers, and a new government could make those efforts harder to sustain even if Israel’s policies on the ground barely shift.
The paths from here

What would a Jewish-Arab government actually change? Natan Sachs, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute in Washington, flatly rejected the idea that an Eisenkot government would be no different from Netanyahu’s. It’s true that both want Hamas gone and Iran boxed in, and that neither is going to offer the Palestinians a state anytime soon. But Eisenkot, Sachs told me, would be slower to use force, would treat Arab citizens as part of the country rather than a threat, and would reverse the damage Netanyahu has done to the courts and the civil service.
There is enormous pressure to reach a deal rather than go back to the polls.

Palestinian citizens turned out in huge numbers to make a former IDF chief prime minister, he said, “because they see the difference, so I would defer to them.” A coalition with Arab parties wouldn’t end the occupation or freeze settlements, but it would take the West Bank away from Smotrich and Ben-Gvir, the two ministers who’ve pushed hardest for annexation.

Even a short-lived Jewish-Arab coalition would matter, Jabareen of Adalah told me. “Even if it’s just for one or one and a half years, they can do a lot of things,” he said, pointing to forming a state commission of inquiry into the security failures before October 7, repealing Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul, and appointing Supreme Court justices. Beyond that, Arab leaders want to be inside the government to make sure its budgets reach their communities, with more money to fight violence and invest in construction and jobs.

Even before a governing coalition forms, the Jewish opposition parties can work with Ra’am and the Joint List in parliament, which convenes on November 10. Together they hold 67 of 120 seats, enough to pass laws and make appointments even without controlling the government. The first test will be replacing Netanyahu’s handpicked speaker, who controls what comes to a vote, which everyone in the opposition wants.

Almost any governing coalition will require some of the Jewish opposition leaders to break a campaign promise or two. The experts I interviewed were divided on how much that practically matters at this stage, and several noted it would hardly be the first time an Israeli politician had reneged. Eisenkot could also turn to the ultra-Orthodox parties, though that would likely mean compromising on the military draft exemptions his whole alliance campaigned against. President Donald Trump and Israeli President Isaac Herzog may also push for a so-called unity government with Eisenkot and Netanyahu. Whatever Eisenkot chooses, there is enormous pressure to reach a deal rather than go back to the polls, because few expect Arab citizens or the Israelis who flew in from abroad to turn out the same way in a repeat election, and a lower turnout would likely favor Netanyahu.
Kor, the campaigner who worked for Golan’s party, said what the moment requires is courage.
“Centrist leaders have shown an alarming amount of passivity,” he told me. “There’s been a lack of willingness to carry people and lead.”

articles.headline: Control of Congress is at stake today. And, judge to consider motion in Clancy case
keyFacts: Voters head to the polls today in an election with record spending that could result in Democrats regaining control of Congress.
A Massachusetts judge will announce a decision later this month on whether to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy.
The U.S. Supreme Court rejected a DOJ request to halt California from processing ballots for thousands of likely noncitizens.
body: Control of Congress is at stake today. And, judge to consider motion in Clancy case
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories

Election Day has arrived. This campaign has the biggest price tag in U.S. history. A record number of lawmakers are stepping down, setting the stage for Democrats to potentially regain control of Congress. All the while, President Trump's popularity is at an all-time low. Here's everything you need to know about today's election, and four types of House races to watch as results come in. NPR has your guide for how to watch the results and when polls close, hour by hour.

- 🎧 The president's unpopular policies have rocked the economy and made unexpected states like Arkansas, Kansas, Mississippi and Iowa crucial for deciding control of Congress, NPR's Stephen Fowler tells Up First. Voters are concerned about the war in Iran, rising gas prices and issues like corruption. They expressed feeling neglected by Trump's focus on grand events instead of their priorities. Both parties are investing heavily in numerous House races. Republicans' closing message asked for two more years to fix issues, and Democrats argued they have already had too much time.

- 🎧 Trump said yesterday that if a portion of his supporters voted, they could win in a "landslide," but he appeared to recognize the challenges ahead, NPR's Franco Ordoñez says. He spoke in the past tense, which is unlike his usual bombast. Results could take days, and Trump's team will closely monitor Republican turnout in crucial Senate races in places like Ohio, Kansas and South Carolina, where polls will close sooner. Strong turnout might ease Trump's worries, but close races in South Carolina or Florida could signal a tough night for Republicans, Ordoñez says.
- ➡️ Race calls are crucial on election night. Here's how NPR collaborates with the Associated Press to make them.

- ➡️ Just before Election Day, NPR conducted one final check-in with swing voters for its Swing Shift project. All of them have cast a vote for Trump in the past decade. They're now rating his presidency while considering their choice when he isn't on the ballot.

- ➡️ The U.S. Supreme Court rejected the Department of Justice's last-minute request to intervene in its unprecedented feud with California over voter rolls. The DOJ sought to halt California from processing ballots for thousands of individuals identified as "likely" noncitizens.

- ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Iran has been leveraging the U.S. midterms in its pressure campaign to push Trump back to negotiations. The elections could signal a possible return to conflict with the U.S. and Israel. The Associated Press reports that the U.S. conducted defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz last night, including Qeshm Island, which is a key launch point for Iran's strikes. While NPR could not independently confirm the details, Iran reported explosions on the island. This pattern of strikes has occurred several times in recent months, coinciding with heightened Iranian attacks on shipping vessels in the Strait.

- 🎧 Iranian officials say they prefer to return to negotiations. The country has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days ahead of the seven it proposed in September, if the U.S. re-engages in talks, NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi says. The Iranian inflation rate is around 90%, and residents are facing dire economic conditions alongside fears of potential bombings. As winter approaches, officials are urging millions of Iranians to conserve energy to avoid soaring natural gas prices. They say the country's natural gas networks are unstable due to damage from the war. Al-Shalchi says Tehran is hoping it can wait out the U.S. election and possibly see Trump's party lose control of Congress.

A Massachusetts judge is considering a motion to dismiss the case against Lindsay Clancy. Plymouth Superior Court Judge William Sullivan will announce his decision later this month. In court yesterday, Clancy's attorney requested that the judge dismiss the case or initiate a new trial. Clancy faces first-degree murder charges for the 2023 deaths of her three young children in their Duxbury home. The trial ended in a mistrial in September when jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict. The Plymouth County district attorney's office has not disclosed its next steps, including whether to seek a new trial or pursue lesser charges. In a recent motion, prosecutors stated they aim to "pursue justice" for Clancy's children.
Picture show

The Siena Drone Photo Awards showcase aerial views of our planet each year, highlighting landscapes and human stories often hidden from view. Photographer George Steinmetz won the top prize of 2026 for his photo titled "Shipbreaking on the mudflats, Bay of Bengal," which captures a stranded vessel off the coast of Bangladesh. The image depicts workers around a partially dismantled tanker designed for transporting liquefied natural gas. The photo illustrates the country's shipbreaking industry, where enormous vessels from around the globe are dismantled, and their materials are repurposed. See Steinmetz's work and some of this year's winning and highly commended photographs from countries in the Global South.
Behind the story
by Jonaki Mehta, education correspondent focused on disabilities and learning differences

For half a century, America hasn't had enough special education teachers. It's a shortage that's only gotten worse as the number of students with disabilities grows rapidly — 8.2 million according to the most recent federal count, or about 1 in 6 students.

Research explains some of why these roles are so hard to fill: These teachers enjoy working with students but spend more time on legally required paperwork and tasks other than teaching. They often don't get paid more despite having more responsibilities than many other teachers. And because there's such a widespread shortage, the teachers who stay in the profession are often handed a bigger load.

NPR wanted to go beyond the research and hear directly from educators, so NPR senior producer Lauren Migaki and I have been exchanging voice memos with more than a dozen teachers from big and small districts around the country. So far, they've shared tales of joy when a student found success, tearful moments when they felt like they had failed, and waking up before dawn to make sure they were prepared.

For example, Jeffrey Carroll, who teaches in Newport News, Va., said last year, he was teaching students across three grade levels and multiple subjects: second, fourth and fifth. It meant he was constantly running from one classroom to the next. "I just didn't feel like I was teaching, I was never in a class long enough to be a meaningful part of it." This year, he was relieved to only be teaching across two grade levels. "It's been good to support my students in the classroom. I get to do some co-teaching. The lesson plans come to life."
Lauren and I will stay in touch with these teachers throughout the rest of the school year and visit some in their classrooms to get a better understanding of what it takes to do this essential job.
3 things to know before you go

- The National Symphony Orchestra is currently without a home while its Kennedy Center venue is involved in a federal court dispute. The NSO faced a new reality when it had to find six alternative concert venues in the Washington, D.C., area while hoping to maintain its budget amid ongoing controversies.
- After entertaining visitors for decades at the St. Louis Zoo, Raja, a 10,000-pound Asian elephant, has moved to new stomping grounds at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden. (via STLPR)
- The Commonwealth of Virginia and the District of Columbia have filed a lawsuit to stop the construction of Trump's proposed 250-foot-tall triumphal arch.

articles.headline: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
keyFacts: US officials told CBS that the US carried out limited and defensive strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in response to Iranian forces firing on a US aircraft.
The strikes occurred as mediators intensified efforts to prevent a return to full-scale war following the US midterm elections.
Iranian and US sides are currently reviewing proposals through Qatari and Pakistani mediators to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
body: - Published
The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The US military has not commented on the strikes, which came as mediators stepped up their efforts to prevent a return to all-out war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Earlier on Monday, the president told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.

"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."
He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.

There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".

Meanwhile, the Associated Press cited two regional officials as saying that, during a weekend phone call, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran following the midterms.
On Tuesday, Iran's chief negotiator with the US, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, stated: "The ball is now in America's court to prevent war."
"Just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response," he said in a televised speech.

It was not immediately clear what Ghalibaf was referring to, but Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Irna on Monday that "very intensive" talks to try to end the war were under way with the US via Qatari and Pakistani mediators.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.
"Both parties remain committed to the negotiation process... We are facilitating the real-time exchange of proposals between them," Majed al-Ansari told reporters in Doha.

Last week, Iranian negotiators discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions. They reportedly include lifting a naval blockade of Iranian ports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.headline: Beyond the hype: AI, not for AI’s sake
keyFacts: Enterprise AI success is defined by solving genuine business problems rather than deploying the most powerful models simply for the sake of it.
Businesses are finding that simpler technologies like traditional machine learning or conventional automation are often more effective and cheaper than complex LLMs.
Competitive advantage in enterprise AI will come from technical restraint and choosing the right tool based on data and desired outcomes.
body: Business leaders, governments, and tech giants are locked in a high-stakes race for AI supremacy, fueled by debates over the destructive power of superintelligence. In this sort of arena, it’s essential that enterprises stay grounded and resist the urge to start a race of their own, deploying ever-larger models simply for the sake of it.
AI/ML Engineering Lead at Beyond.

In the context of enterprise AI, there is no prize for launching the most powerful model first, building the highest number of agents, or forcing AI into every workflow. True success is defined by solving genuine business problems and delivering outcomes that justify the underlying cost and complexity.

While the prospect of a single, omnipotent large language model (LLM) is inspiring, today's business realities demand a more measured approach: every problem has a right tool, and often, that tool is a simple one.
AI doesn't have to mean LLMs

Before generative AI dominated the conversation, businesses were already using machine learning for recommendations, forecasting, fraud detection and estimating things such as the lifetime value of a customer.

We have had years to understand these technologies, including how to deploy and monitor them and make predictions at scale quickly and cheaply. An LLM may be capable of tackling some of the same problems, but that doesn't always make it the better option. More sophisticated models can cost considerably more to run and introduce variability that is unnecessary for a straightforward prediction.

Sometimes AI isn't necessary at all. If a process follows known rules and needs to produce the same result every time (moving data between systems on a schedule or triggering an action when a predefined condition is met, for example), conventional automation may do the job perfectly well.

Long before agents arrived, businesses handled these tasks with pipelines, schedulers, and rules. If that approach is reliable, fast, and inexpensive, adding an AI agent doesn't make the process more intelligent; it can simply make it more complex.

Generative AI earns its place when creativity or interpretation are required: understanding language or images, for example, or handling a process where the next step changes according to context. Agents can go further by using that understanding to interact with systems and take actions, opening up processes that were previously extremely difficult to automate.
The future is likely to combine conventional automation, traditional ML, generative AI and agents, rather than one replacing everything that came before it.
The AI honeymoon is ending

These distinctions matter more as enterprise AI moves beyond experimentation. A proof of concept can demonstrate what a model or agent is capable of, but production introduces running costs, security, monitoring and the work required to keep increasingly autonomous systems under control.
An engineer once gave me an analogy that captures this well. Imagine growing a tree that you need to maintain in a particular shape. When a branch grows in the wrong direction, you cut it.

Then another appears elsewhere. The difficult part is finding all the branches. Developing an agent can be similar. Obvious behaviors can be controlled relatively quickly, but real-world use exposes edge cases that weren't visible during development.

The more freedom a system has to interpret information and make decisions, the more important evaluation, monitoring and guardrails become. Control needs to extend beyond model behavior to the data a system can access, the actions it is authorized to take, the information it retains and the point at which a human can intervene.

There is also cost to consider. The most capable models can be expensive at scale, so additional capability needs to create enough additional value to justify it. As experimentation gives way to scrutiny of ROI, businesses will become less interested in whether something can use AI and more interested in whether AI actually leads to an improved commercial or operational outcome enough to justify the cost.
Let the data decide
Avoiding over-engineering starts with the business need and the data, rather than choosing the technology first.

Data engineers and analysts are crucial because they understand where information comes from, how reliable it is and what it can actually tell you. AI and ML engineers can put mathematical models on top, but sophistication cannot compensate for data that doesn't support the task.
The data and desired outcome will often point towards the appropriate approach. Fast, reliable predictions from structured numerical data may be better suited to traditional ML.

Language, images and other unstructured information can make generative AI valuable, while processes that require human level understanding to trigger actions across different systems may justify agents.
And sometimes conventional software will remain the best answer. Starting with “we need an agent” and then looking for a problem to give it is the wrong way around.
The right people matter as much as the technology

Increasingly capable AI has also created an assumption that businesses will inevitably need fewer engineers. AI is certainly changing productivity: experienced engineers can complete work faster with these tools, while junior engineers who learn to use them effectively can become productive more quickly.

But businesses still need people who understand what is happening underneath. I like to compare it with smartphones. Most of us use a phone effectively without being able to explain the hardware, operating system and networks behind it. That doesn't mean the underlying engineering skills have disappeared. Somebody still needs to understand those systems.

AI is likely to develop in a similar way. Many people will become highly capable users, while businesses will still need engineers with the deeper technical knowledge to build, control and fix the systems underneath.

That means continuing to invest in junior talent too. Senior engineers eventually move companies, change roles or retire. Organizations still need mentorship and knowledge transfer so today's juniors become tomorrow's senior engineers.
The opportunity isn't people or AI, but the two together. Capable engineers equipped with these tools can achieve considerably more than either could independently.
The next AI advantage will be restraint

The wider battle over superintelligence and increasingly powerful models will continue, but it shouldn't dictate how enterprises make technology decisions. To make this technical restraint viable in practice, engineering leaders must actively manage executive and board-level fear of missing out, turning top-down pressure for a visible ‘AI strategy’ into discipline, value-driven execution.

Some business problems will justify sophisticated AI tools. Agents will make previously impractical forms of automation possible, while generative AI can transform how organizations work with language, images and unstructured information. Others will be solved perfectly well by traditional ML, conventional automation or straightforward software.

Knowing the difference will become increasingly valuable. Competitive advantage will come from knowing where AI materially improves an outcome, where a simpler technology is more effective and how to move the right systems into productions securely and economically.

That requires good data, strong engineering talent and enough technical judgement to resist complexity simply because it is available. In the next phase of enterprise AI, restraint will not signal a lack of ambition, instead it will be a sign of technical maturity.

articles.headline: UK food supply chain affected by European freezer hacks, cyber chief says
keyFacts: UK food supply chain businesses have been impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe, the National Cyber Security Centre said.
The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers stated some members became collateral in the hacks, though no meat was lost.
NCSC chief executive Dr Richard Horne said it was too early to say who was behind the attacks and urged organizations to invest in technology security.
body: - Published
Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."
The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.
The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) has told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.

"None who have been affected have lost any meat but once again this must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be see by some as targets," said Tony Goodger, head of communications at AIMS.
"We urge our members and the wider industry to be vigilant."
It comes after supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges being hiked in temperature on Monday.
The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.
Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.
Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.
But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.

"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.
Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.
But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".
"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.
"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."
Thrown away food
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected in Monday's cyber incident, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up.
The same method was thought to have been used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
As with that incident, many of the retailers affected on Monday said they had no choice but to throw away spoiled food - some saying it amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro in lost produce.
Mathieu Tilman, who runs a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, told the BBC he found it "truly distressing".
"There's so many people starving, people who don't have enough to eat. How can we end up throwing away so much food?"
"In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
So far, there have been little to no signs of any such impact in the UK.
But the BBC has approached major UK supermarkets for comment and asked what action, if any, they are taking to safeguard against any similar hacks attempts.

"Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks," said Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.
Asda, Lidl, M&S, Sainsbury's and Tesco are among the retail trade association's members.

articles.headline: US midterm elections 2026 live: Americans go to the polls in referendum on Trump’s agenda
keyFacts: Americans are voting in the 2026 midterm elections to decide control of Congress and 39 governorships during the final two years of Trump's term.
Key voter issues include the economy, immigration, artificial intelligence, and soaring fuel prices driven by the conflict with Iran.
Voting is taking place on Tuesday, but the final outcome could be delayed by close races, different state counting rules, and potential recounts.
body: What is being decided in the midterms and why do they matter?
David Smith

The US Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and theSenate. Both must approve federal legislation before it can become law and both play important roles in overseeing the executive branch.

The House is elected every two years, meaning all 435 voting seats are contested at every congressional election. The Senate has 100 members serving staggered six-year terms, so roughly a third of its seats are up for election every two years.
This year’s ballot includes:
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives. Republicans are defending a narrow majority, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

35 seats in the Senate. Thirty-three seats are up in regular elections, along with two special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill the remainder of terms that were vacated early. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, against 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them. Democrats need to gain four seats to secure a majority.
39 governorships. Voters will choose governors in 36 states and three US territories.
Thousands of state legislative seats, as well as local offices, judicial contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules.

The elections for Congress will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s second term. The governorships and state legislative contests will shape policymaking closer to home, from education and reproductive rights to taxation and the administration of elections.

The midterms have a long history of punishing the occupant of the White House. The president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterm elections, a 90% rate of loss that stretches back to 1946.
Here are some of the key voter issues shaping the US midterm elections:
The economy: Despite Trump’s 2024 campaign pledge to tackle affordability issues, the economy consistently ranks as voters’ top concern.

Iran: Trump’s decision to go to war with the Tehran regime has exacerbated economic worries. Iran’s retaliatory decision to close the strait of Hormuz has driven up gasoline prices for US motorists. It also represents a breach of his pledge to end the US’s supposed addiction to “forever wars”.

Immigration: Enforcement and closing the border remains a signature issue for Trump. He repeatedly boasts of the impact of his closure of the southern border as one of his biggest achievements, making comparisons with the performance of Joe Biden.

AI and datacenters: AI has emerged as a key campaign issue, with surveys showing a majority of voters holding negative views on it, even as Trump champions its development and attempts to rename it “super intelligence”.
You can read more about the issues guiding the elections here:

A final set of polls from the New York Times and Siena University, published on Sunday, put Democratic candidates ahead in five of seven key battleground contests – including Texas and Kansas, where voters have not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988 and 1932, respectively.

The final stretch of the campaign was not without drama for the Democrats, however. In Michigan – widely seen as a crucial pillar to either party’s ambitions of control in the Senate – Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost her party’s senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, on Sunday.

Stevens was widely condemned by fellow Democrats over the move, which followed a feud with the El-Sayed campaign over an outside group’s campaign ad that blamed the high cost of living on US support for Israel. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, described her endorsement of Rogers as “a despicable betrayal”.
“Whatever they’re trying to distract you, it’s because they’re picking your pocket,” El-Sayed told hundreds of supporters in Royal Oak, Michigan on Monday.

The extraordinary rupture in Michigan took places days after the party faced damaging headlines in Alaska, where it was reported that the Democratic senate candidate’s campaign was behind an effort to recruit a challenger with almost the same name as her rival, the Republican senator Dan Sullivan. (The Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, has denied any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign.)

Before the report of the Peltola campaign’s involvement, the Department of Justice (DoJ) filed a lawsuit to block the certification of Alaska’s Senate results in the event of a Republican defeat, citing potential “voter confusion” over the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. The lawsuit has since been dismissed by a judge.

Voting is taking place today (Tuesday 3 November), but the results may not be known tonight. Close contests, different state rules for counting early and postal ballots, and possible recounts or legal challenges could delay the final outcome.

Once the dust has settled, there will be no respite in this – the land of the endless campaign. Attention will soon turn to the 2028 presidential election campaign, when both parties will seek to turn the results of this November into a foundation for the next fight for the White House.
Here’s an hour-by-hour rundown of when polls close around the US, courtesy of our blogger and reporter Shrai Popat:
The first polls have opened in the pivotal US midterm elections in the eastern state of Vermont, where it has just gone past 5.15am.
The next polls to open will be at 6am ET (in 40 minutes) including in: Connecticut, Indiana, Kentucky, Maine, New Jersey, New York and Virginia.
The first results will start to come in after 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT) but a tight race could take hours to call – or even days.

It is important to remember that more than 58m early votes have already been cast across the US, according to an analysis by the University of Florida, a huge increase in the total number of early votes made in the last midterm elections, in 2022.
Rachel Leingang, a Midwest political correspondent for Guardian US, has been in Iowa, getting a sense of the political mood ahead of the crcuial elections:

Across Iowa on Monday, candidates made final pitches in a set of toss-up races up and down the ballot, noting just how close these contests were and how pivotal the state could be for the nation’s politics.

In a standing-room-only town hall in Waverly, Iowa, Democratic gubernatorial hopeful Rob Sand started off by asking people in the crowd which political party they belong to, then having people clap for all of them before directing the audience to sing “America the Beautiful” together.
The bipartisan tone underscores Sand’s pitch to Iowa voters, including those who would need to cross party lines to support him: “not redder or bluer, but better and truer”.

Wearing shirts that urged people to vote for Democrats and “rotate the crops”, about 150 voters turned out to the rally in the Republican-leaning area. Sand told the Guardian that throughout the hundreds of town halls he has seen a “yearning” from people for their politicians to work together to solve problems, even as voters are generally angry this year.

“We need to focus that anger and point it at where it ought to be pointed, which is at a broken two-choice political system that is too easily abused to allow elected officials to be corrupt and to be lazy and still hold power,” he said. “A lot of politicians want people to be angry with their neighbors.”

Down in the Des Moines suburbs in the early evening, as rain poured down and the sun set before 6pm, Sarah Booz knocked doors for Democratic candidates. On the doors, there were still a lot of undecided voters.

Some told her they’d be voting for Sand and the rest of the downballot Democrats, while others said they needed to do more research. One man who said he normally votes red said the gubernatorial race would probably be a last-minute decision.

And in the evening, at a Holiday Inn by the Des Moines airport, much of the Republican ticket rallied, culminating in a pitch from US Senate candidate Ashley Hinson. Chuck Grassley, the Republican US senator and the oldest sitting US senator, took digs at Sand, saying that the state government is well run and “we don’t need Sand in that machinery”. He also called Democrats running across the country “outlandish socialists” who want to “transform America”.

“I hope that you’ll do everything you can to make sure that I have a colleague from Iowa that won’t neutralize my vote,” he said, advocating for Hinson. Hinson, taking the stage in front of a bus she’s been campaigning in, called her opponent, Zach Turek, “Too Liberal Turek”. “We fire liberal phonies, we don’t promote them,” she said.
US strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island on eve of midterm elections
The US reportedly attacked Qeshm Island in southern Iran on Monday after Donald Trump downplayed the chances of a return to war with Tehran after the midterm elections.
“We had a war with Iran. We won,” Trump told journalists yesterday. “I don’t know if you even call it a war because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.”

Monday’s strikes, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, were defensive in nature, according to officials, and targeted surface-to-air missiles being used against US assets, Reuters and the Associated Press reported.

But undermining Trump’s comments to the press, the WSJ reported that the US has been launching smaller-scale strikes against Iran for several weeks, but have not been publicly announcing the attacks as they did at the start of the conflict in February.

On Monday, US vice-president JD Vance claimed there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians” and that he was feeling good about the prospects of a “negotiated settlement”. But despite this talk of diplomatic progress, Iran has continued to enforce its closure of the strait of Hormuz and in recent weeks Trump has hinted at renewing attacks on Iran after the midterm elections are over.
Voters now have the chance to express their frustration over the inflationary impact of the president’s ill-judged war, which has sent fuel prices soaring and shown the limits of American power.
