articles.headline: It looks like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 had fewer active players at launch in the US compared to last year's Black Ops 7
keyFacts: Circana data shows Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 had lower launch player engagement on PlayStation and Xbox in the US compared to last year's Black Ops 7.
Analyst Mat Piscatella reported that Modern Warfare 4 achieved 19 percent engagement on PlayStation, 17 percent on Xbox, and 4.2 percent on Steam during its launch week.
Analysts noted that the drop on Xbox may be due to Modern Warfare 4 lacking a day-one release on Game Pass.
body: It's been speculated for a while that Call of Duty may be losing its lustre. Although we don't have concrete data with detailed statistics for each game released in the last several years, there's an observable trend in player numbers that's hard to ignore.
US market analysis firm Circana published some data showing player engagement with Modern Warfare 4 following its launch, and compared them to those by Black Ops 7.

The data is based on Circana's proprietary Player Engagement Tracker, which tracks player activity in the US across Steam and PlayStation, and worldwide on Xbox. According to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, 19 percent of players on PlayStation played Modern Warfare 4 in the week ending 24th October, compared to 17 percent on Xbox, and 4.2 percent on Steam.

With the exception of Steam, those numbers are down compared to last year's Black Ops 7, which saw 23 percent engagement on PlayStation, 29 percent on Xbox, and a meagre 1.5 percent on Steam during its launch week.

Call of Duty managed to land in the top 10 across all three platforms during the same week ending 24th October, per Circana. In fact, it sat just below Fortnite on PlayStation, which is a decent result.

The large drop in activity on Xbox could be explained by Modern Warfare 4's lack of a day-one release on Game Pass. Black Ops 7 was the second (and last) Call of Duty to launch on Game Pass day-and-date with its premium release. Game Pass availability typically boosts player numbers, though not always sales.

The drop on PlayStation is a little harder to explain, but could be a side effect of the incredibly successful Black Ops 1 & 2 ports released in the summer on PS4 and PS5, which captured lapsed players who may have simply lost interest in modern Call of Duty, regardless of the perceived quality of Modern Warfare 4.

Judging by the data we have access to, such as SteamDB numbers showing Modern Warfare 4's launch compared to Black Ops 7's and other recent releases, there's evidence this year's game perhaps isn't as popular as it could've been.

Indeed, even Activision's tenor when talking about Call of Duty first weekend sales has changed. The publisher issued a single statement following Modern Warfare 4's launch, through Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, which does not even mention the game by name.

"One of the most celebrated Call of Duty games in its 24-year history, and now $40bn in lifetime franchise revenue," Sharma wrote on X. "An incredible milestone. Congrats to the Activision team. And to the players, thank you for being with us."
Last year's Black Ops 7 post-launch statement sidestepped talk of sales and revenue entirely, insteading praising the "great response to the quality and depth of gameplay in Black Ops 7".

articles.headline: U.S. to mediate new round of Ukraine-Russia talks, Witkoff says
keyFacts: U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff stated that the United States will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11.
Witkoff noted that American negotiators will meet with European and NATO representatives this week to discuss future security guarantees for Ukraine.
Authorities reported that recent Russian strikes across Ukraine killed at least 29 people in Zaporizhzhia and wounded 25 people at a medical facility in Kharkiv.
body: The U.S. will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in November, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Tuesday night. In a post on X, Witkoff said the discussions on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi would "focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

He added that American negotiators would meet this week with representatives from European allies and the NATO alliance, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to discuss future security guarantees for Ukraine, which has been one of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recurring demands for any deal with Russia.

"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said.

Ukraine and Russia have held several rounds of talks mediated by the U.S. during President Trump's second term, often yielding prisoner exchanges or other low-level agreements, but Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite some administration, has thus far refused to drop his demand for Ukraine to accept Russia's unilateral annexation of some territory siezed over the course of the grueling war.

Zelenskyy, likewise, has consistently ruled out accepting Russia's seizure of territory by force, and many U.S. allies in Europe agree that legitimizing Putin's landgrab would set a dangerous precedent.

Witkoff's latest announcement of planned talks at the working level — which generally means discussions among technocrats, not at the senior diplomatic or national leadership level — comes after a rare, localized ceasefire in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson ended on Sunday.
The brief truce allowed humanitarian supplies into the small Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and the of an undisclosed number of residents.
The ceasefire, credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo, has raised some hope for more diplomatic progress toward ending the on Feb. 24, 2022.
Russia has continued pummeling the rest of Ukraine during and after the local ceasefire, however, with more strikes coming overnight into Tuesday across the country.
At least 29 people were killed in a village in the southeast Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia, authorities said Tuesday.
In the northeast city of Kharkiv, the regional administration said a Russia strike hit a medical facility, wounding 25 people and forcing the evacuation of around 200 patients.
Russia's defense ministry said Tuesday that it had carried out a "massive strike" on energy facilities across Ukraine, and port infrastructure in the Odessa region.
Moscow's mayor said, meanwhile, that 500 Ukrainian drones heading toward the capital were destroyed overnight.

articles.headline: West Ham approach Parker after sacking boss Nuno
keyFacts: West Ham United sacked head coach Nuno Espirito Santo following a disappointing start to the Championship season and relegation from the Premier League.
BBC Sport understands that West Ham are in advanced talks to appoint former Bournemouth and Burnley boss Scott Parker as their new head coach.
Mark Noble, Steve Potts, and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of the team for their upcoming Championship match against Cardiff City.
body: - Published
West Ham United are expected to appoint Scott Parker as head coach after sacking Nuno Espirito Santo.
The 52-year-old Portuguese head coach has paid the price for West Ham's disappointing start to the Championship season, having overseen their relegation from the Premier League last season.
BBC Sport understands that the club are in advanced talks with former Burnley, Bournemouth and Fulham boss Parker and he could be confirmed before Wednesday's Championship trip to Cardiff City.
The former England midfielder had four seasons as a player with the Hammers and led Bournemouth and Burnley to promotion from the Championship as a manager.
Widely seen as favourites for automatic promotion, the London side are currently eighth in the table, six points behind leaders Middlesbrough.

They have won two of their past six games and have lost back-to-back home matches - going down 3-2 to Southampton and then 3-1 to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday - losses that have seen them drop down from second place.
Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also left the club.
Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of the side for their Championship trip to Cardiff City on Wednesday night.

"Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club's objectives and expectations remain on track," a West Ham United statement read.
"West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future.
"The process of recruiting a new head coach is already under way."
The decision means West Ham are looking for their fourth permanent manager since David Moyes left London Stadium in May 2024.
His successor Julen Lopetegui was sacked after just six months in charge with the Hammers mid-table having won six of their 20 Premier League matches.
He was replaced by former Chelsea and Brighton boss Graham Potter, who oversaw a 14th-placed finish, but was sacked after only eight months in charge with the club 19th in the table.

The club opted to stick with former Wolves and Tottenham Hotspur boss Nuno despite him being unable to turn around the club's fortunes. They were relegated at the end of last season after finishing two points behind Spurs.
Despite that, this season had a troubled start for the Hammers - they failed to win any of their first three league matches and were 19th in the table.

A run of four successive wins in the first half of September, where they scored 16 goals and went top of the table, appeared to show they had adapted to the second tier, with a 6-0 win over Wrexham the highlight of the run.
Just two league victories have come since - a 6-0 win at nine-man Lincoln City and a 1-0 victory at Swansea City followed draws with London rivals Millwall and QPR.
A squad that Parker can work with?
Having posted losses of more than Â£104m, relegation meant West Ham had to sell players over the summer.
The departures of the likes of Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville, El Hadji Malick Diouf, James Ward-Prowse and Freddie Potts secured the club about Â£150m in transfer revenue.
They used some of that cash to pay Celtic a Championship record Â£22m for midfielder Arne Engels and spent a reported Â£12m on Norwegian winger Edvin Austbo.

Experienced campaigners Joel Veltman and Manor Solomon also joined on free transfers from Brighton and Tottenham respectively while they kept key players such as England winger Jarrod Bowen, Czech midfielder Tomas Soucek and Greek defender Konstantinos Mavropanos.

Soucek missed the first two months of the season with an ankle injury while some of their other signings have yet to deliver. Engels has three assists and no goals in 12 games while Austbo has scored twice and had two assists having started just two league matches.
It is a squad that is capable of turning things around, especially under a manager with Championship promotion experience such as Parker.
'West Ham's hierarchy feel Parker understands the club'
Analysis - Simon Stone, BBC Sport chief football news reporter
Given the estimated Â£200m loss in revenue it is imperative the club goes straight back up to the Premier League.
Two wins in six, a run which has dropped West Ham to eighth in the table, four points off second-placed Swansea in the final automatic promotion place, is not good enough.
Scott Parker is the obvious choice as replacement and West Ham are wasting no time in getting the deal done.

Parker made 129 appearances in a four-year stint with the Hammers. He won the club's player of the year award three times and was at West Ham when he was named Football Writers' Association player of the year in 2011.
West Ham's hierarchy feel Parker understands the club and the culture and is someone the fans can get behind.
Equally as important, he has already been promoted from the Championship three times, at Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley.
West Ham will hope he makes it number four next May.
'The expectation is for an immediate return to the Premier League'
Analysis - Phil Parry, BBC Radio London sport editor

There were some who thought that Nuno would leave the club in the summer after they failed to survive their relegation battle, but the stability that he offered and his experience of guiding Wolves out of the Championship were seen as positive reasons to welcome his continuation at the helm.
The 6-0 thumpings handed out to Wrexham and Lincoln are contrasted with some disappointing home defeats, including the past two outings at London Stadium.
One of the major concerns has been the slow starts to games. They have conceded the opening goal in four of their past six in the Championship and have picked up just two points from those matches.
It has been suggested that the team just don't appear to appreciate the intensity and urgency of games at this level and are still a little too ponderous in the first half.
The Hammers have just been through a run of matches against teams who are in good form and are sitting high in the table, but losses in two of those games, both at home, have proven costly for Nuno.

With the squad at their disposal and the fanbase that backs them, it will be an attractive job for the next head coach, but whoever it is will be aware that the expectation at London Stadium is for an immediate return to the Premier League and falling short of that objective is risky for long-term prospects.

articles.headline: Campaign to keep Ilhan Omar’s secrets safe includes threats against anyone who speaks out: ‘You’ll be killed … snake’
keyFacts: Members of the Somali community face online threats and physical violence from a protective group when they speak out about US Representative Ilhan Omar.
One critic told The Post he was physically assaulted in Minneapolis and Kenya after speaking to the press about Omar.
The New York Post reported that the protective group is not officially connected to Omar, and she is not accused of any wrongdoing.
body: Few members of the tight-knit Somali community are willing to talk about Ilhan Omar — due to threats and fear of violence if they do.

The Minnesota representative is backed by a fiercely protective group, many of whom take it upon themselves to bombard anyone who speaks out with online threats and even physical harm in the US, Europe and Africa.
The group is not officially connected to Omar, and do not receive instructions from her and it is unclear if she is personally aware of their actions.
The Post understands one member of the community who broke ranks was assaulted on the streets of Minneapolis and again in Kenya after their name appeared in the press.
The critic was attacked outside a Kenyan restaurant in 2022 and left with a concussion as well as several cuts and bruises.
“I got jumped by 15 people and was pepper-sprayed,” the man, who asked not to be named for fear of further retribution, told The Post.
“After that I don’t really remember what happened. All I know is I was thrown to the ground and had so many punches and kicks thrown at me.
The man believes the attack was sparked by a popular Somali TikTok star, who described the critic as a “fool” and threatened to “punch him in the face” if he ever comes to Minnesota.
“I was attacked because of this man. He set his followers on me after sharing my location,” he claimed.
In separate videos, the TikTokker tells his loyal fans: “There are people in our community who have snitched on Ilhan Omar, as well as gone after her father.
“People have looked the other way for too long, you bitches.”

Local Minnesota journalists have encountered problems reporting on Omar since she was first elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives in 2016. The notoriously protective and tight-knit community was quick to hurl accusations of racism at anything that questioned her background, policies or turbulent personal life, sources told The Post.

Omar first came to Minnesota as a refugee in 1995, escaping the bloody civil war in Somalia. She has faced allegations she fraudulently married her second husband — also her alleged brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi — for immigration purposes. They married in 2009 and split around 2012, but did not divorce until 2017.

Meanwhile, one Post source within the community received a chilling phone call, telling him to recant anything he had ever said about Omar and to instead issue statements of support for her ahead of the midterms.
“I feel very threatened for simply disagreeing with anything to do with Ilhan Omar,” the source claimed.
“If you don’t support her, then these people online really want to make you pay. I am fearful of my life every single day. I wish I never said anything about her.
“I get death wishes every day, and I am afraid to leave my home. On the rare occasions I do, I am verbally abused or, worse, actually physically assaulted.”
Only a handful of people in the Somali community have been willing to publicly share what they know about Omar’s relationship with Elmi since it first came to light.
One man based in Somalia, known as Aardile, claimed to have put a hit out on the Minnesota man who was quoted speaking negatively about Omar in a report.
“We are sending people after you, they’re going to put you in hospital and in a coma,” he proudly stated in a video online.
“My heart sank when I heard that because these people are not a joke, they’re dangerous,” the source told The Post.
“I stayed in bed for the entire week and could not face going outside in fear of being shot dead at any moment.”
Another outright told him “you are going to be killed” and labelled him a “snake.”
The Post also heard a chilling seven-minute phone call made by a “leading member” of the Somali community in the city to someone speaking against the congresswoman.
The source was explicitly told to say “I lied about Omar because we were arguing” and to publish a message of support for her ahead of the elections.
The source — who also asked not to be named — ultimately refused, but said he felt pressured because he didn’t want to be “villainized in the community” further.
None of the social media trolls are linked to Omar and she is not accused of any wrongdoing. Her office did not respond to a request for comment from The Post.
The congresswoman has vehemently denied that her 2009 marriage was a sham to obtain legal immigration status for Elmi.

articles.headline: Broken promises: Why the Iran war could decide the midterm elections
keyFacts: President Donald Trump departed from his initial anti-war promises by entering into a war with Iran during his second term.
Polls show voter disapproval of Trump's handling of the Iran war ranging from 60% to the upper 60% range.
More than 70% of Americans want Congress to prioritize lowering the cost of living and ending the war in Iran.
body: In his victory speech on election night in 2024, President Donald Trump issued a bold promise. “I’m not going to start a war,” he declared that night almost two years ago, “I’m going to stop wars.” It was a simple but powerful line, reflective of a disruptive and unconventional — not to mention long overdue — shift in American foreign policy.

The promise, as he and others have called it since, was consistent with “America First” — a movement to position the United States away from its role as a global security guarantor and toward a foreign policy guided by the interests of the public. The president’s second term started out strong on this front. But the war with Iran marked a sharp departure from that vision. Certainly, the voters seem to think so.

Heading into the midterm elections, Americans across the political spectrum have sensed a clear shift away from the president’s election night promise on foreign policy. They don’t like what they see.

The voters have not been shy about their displeasure with the president’s foreign policy. Polls in the early months since the war began reflected dissatisfaction in the range of 60%, with concerns about both the war’s immediate economic impacts and the decision to go to war itself. As prospects for a diplomatic solution broke down and the president began threatening major escalation in the summer, voters did not hesitate to make clear the blame they placed on his shoulders. Polling this fall reflected disapproval , with Trump’s handling of the war remaining high in the upper 60% range. With no end to the war in sight, Republican voter negativity toward the president continues trending increasingly higher.
President Donald Trump arrives to board Marine One on the Ellipse near the White House, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026, in Washington. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)

It is widely accepted wisdom in Washington to say that foreign policy is never a top-of-the-ticket issue for American voters. But this midterm election cycle is poised to be an exception. The major polls over the past eight months demonstrate the connection voters are making between the Iran war and its downstream effects on their day-to-day lives, including gas prices and general affordability .

The voters have real reason for their acute disappointment. Trump’s early foreign policy promises teed up a sea change. They signaled a break from the failed policies of Washington’s elites that walked the nation into more than 20 years of seemingly endless wars in the Middle East, traded away critical resources to Ukraine and other partners at the expense of U.S. security, failed to prioritize the rising military threat of China and, at their core, put the security interests of foreign capitals above those of the public.

The president deserves credit for making significant headway to drive and codify the trajectory on which he began his second term. Months into 2025, Trump delivered a historic commitment by NATO allies to spend 5% of GDP on defense, putting the alliance on course to end a decadeslong status quo of American taxpayers subsidizing European security.

In a landmark speech in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, he called out the decades of American adventurism in the Middle East, condemning “nation builders, neocons, and liberal nonprofits” for having “wrecked far more nations than they built,” and wrongly intervening “in complex societies that they did not even understand themselves.”

By the end of his first year back in office, the president’s National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy set the tone for downsizing America’s role in the world with a clear-eyed focus on defined American interests and priorities. War Secretary Pete Hegseth summarized the shift best in his speech to the Reagan National Defense Forum last year, vowing that “the War Department will not be distracted by democracy building interventionism, undefined wars, regime change, climate change, woke moralizing and feckless nation-building. We will instead put our nation’s practical, concrete interests first.”

What has transpired in the administration since those optimistic days hasn’t gone unnoticed by the voters. Nor are they oblivious to the fact that Congress collectively sat idle while Trump waged war unilaterally against Iran for the past eight months. The trendlines do not suggest that voters are offering a pass for the legislative branch’s behavior. One recent survey shows more than 70% of Americans want Congress to prioritize two things in 2027: bringing down the cost of living and ending the war in Iran. That the two are deeply intertwined is a strong signal of how voters are assessing the current state of play in Washington.
GOP TAX CUT SALES PITCH TO VOTERS UNDERCUT BY IRAN AND GAS PRICES

There is no sugarcoating the fact that the president’s decision to go to war with Iran undid his progress toward a foreign policy that reflects the priorities of the American people. He deserves credit for being the first president in the modern era to champion the “America First” vision and challenge the entrenchment and failures of Washington’s foreign policy elites. Yet he also came up short in sticking to it.
The voters have seen that unfold. Expect them to be unforgiving.

Katherine Thompson is a senior fellow in defense and foreign policy studies at the Cato Institute. She most recently held senior positions at the U.S. Department of Defense, including performing the duties of the assistant secretary of defense for international security affairs, where she oversaw policy on Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. She also spent an extensive tenure on Capitol Hill as national security adviser to Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT).

articles.headline: An hour-by-hour guide to watching the 2026 midterms — and when we’ll know who controls Congress
keyFacts: The 2026 midterm election results could be determined anywhere from late Tuesday night to over a week after Election Day depending on how close the races are.
Poll closing times across the United States are staggered by hour, beginning at 6 p.m. ET in parts of Kentucky and Indiana and concluding at 1 a.m. ET in Alaska.
Several high-stakes Senate and gubernatorial races across the country feature toss-ups, ranked-choice voting, or potential litigation that could delay final outcomes.
body: But it can be anywhere from late Tuesday night until over a week after Election Day before the winner becomes clear, depending on how close the House and Senate races will be.
Many forecasters are predicting a blue wave will sweep House races, increasing the odds of knowing who controls the upper chamber late Tuesday or early Wednesday.
In recent history, control of the Senate has been determined fairly quickly, but there are a handful of toss-up races this year, including one in Alaska that could face litigation and drag out.
The Post breaks down when the polls close in key races and what to watch out for:
6 p.m. ET: First polls close in parts of Indiana and Kentucky

The first meaningful signal of the night may come out of Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District. Because the Lexington-area seat sits entirely within the Eastern time zone, its polls are among the earliest in the country to close.

President Trump carried the district by 15 points in 2024, but the race has tightened since, and Fox News’ Power Rankings moved it from Lean R to toss-up. Republican Alvarado faces Democrat Zach Dembo, a former federal prosecutor, for the open seat.
A Democratic flip this early in the evening would be a bad omen for House Republicans.
The seat is open because Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.) is pursuing the Senate seat of the retiring Mitch McConnell. Barr is favored to beat Democrat Charles Booker.
7 p.m. ET: Polls close in Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia

Jackson now faces former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, in a race Cook Political Report rates as a toss-up. A Bottoms victory would make her the first Democrat elected governor of Georgia since Roy Barnes in 1998.

South Carolina is uncharacteristically competitive. Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) was appointed to the Senate in July following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, and later agreed to seek a full term at Trump’s behest. She’s tied with Democrat Annie Andrews at 48% in a New York Times/Siena poll. Fox News has moved the race from Lean R to toss-up.

Virginia should be an early barometer for the House. The state Supreme Court struck down Democrats’ gerrymandered map proposal — which likely would have handed Democrats 10 of the state’s 11 seats — in May, so the old districts are still in place. Even so, Republican Reps. Jen Kiggans and Rob Wittman are defending districts Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger carried in her 2025 landslide.

In Vermont, Gov. Phil Scott — a Republican who won his last race by 52 points, in one of the bluest states in the country — is in a tight race for a sixth two-year term against Democrat Amanda Janoo, an economist. Scott’s immense personal popularity has sagged in recent years, with Vermont Public measuring a 15% approval drop since 2022.
7:30 p.m. ET, polls close in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia
Ohio is starting to look purple again.

Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) led Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) 52% to 47% in a Fox News poll, and Fox moved the race from toss-up to Lean D. The special election will decide who serves the remainder of Vice President JD Vance’s term.
Down ballot, the governor’s race could go down as the GOP’s debacle of the cycle.

Republican Vivek Ramaswamy trails Democrat Amy Acton — who ran Ohio’s COVID response as state health director — by 4.7% in the RealClearPolitics aggregate. Ramaswamy’s most memorable contribution to the race was a $4 million ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter a liar. The mother lost custody when her husband was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12, and Acton accuses her of abuse and neglect. Fellow Republicans, including Gov. Mike DeWine and excluding Trump, condemned the ad.

In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) led former RNC Chairman Michael Whatley (R) 52% to 39% in the final Elon University poll, for the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

8 p.m. ET: Polls close in Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee and Washington, DC

Most of Florida actually closes at 7 p.m., and the state famously counts fast, so two redrawn House seats should offer an early indication. Rep. Kathy Castor’s (D-Fla.) Tampa-area 14th District went from Harris +8 to Trump +11 after redistricting, according to Axios. Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) is defending the 25th District — GOP strategists say a Castor survival would leave Republicans with little hope of holding the House, Axios reported.

Pennsylvania may be where the House is won or lost. Four Republican incumbents face competitive races: Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick, Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan and Scott Perry. Perry is in a rematch with former TV anchor Janelle Stelson, one of the most expensive House contests in the nation. At the top of the ticket, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro is expected to cruise to victory, leading Republican Treasurer Stacy Garrity 59% to 34% in a recent Quinnipiac poll.

Maine’s Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), seeking a sixth term, is the only Republican on the ballot this cycle in a state Kamala Harris mostly won. She’s running against former state Senate President Troy Jackson, who became the Democratic nominee after Graham Platner left the race over sexual assault allegations, which he denies. Jackson led Collins 52% to 47% in a YouGov poll released Sunday. And because Maine uses ranked-choice voting, the race may not be called Tuesday night.

In Mississippi, Republicans are seemingly spooked enough that Trump flew to Corinth on Oct. 26 to rally for Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.). A poll from a lefty firm showed her clinging to a 43% to 40% lead over Democrat Scott Colom. No Democrat has won a Senate race in Mississippi since 1982.
8:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arkansas
The Natural State gets the 8:30 p.m. slot to itself, and Republicans are heavily favored.
9 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, South Dakota, Texas, Wisconsin and Wyoming
The 9 p.m. slot is likely the most decisive for the Senate majority. Most polls in Texas, Michigan and Kansas close at 8 p.m., but the last precincts in each close at 9 p.m.

In Texas, Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) ousted Sen. John Cornyn in a May runoff after a dawdled Trump endorsement. A Fox News poll now has Paxton tied with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico at 49%. No Democrat has won a Senate race in Texas since 1988. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, seeking a fourth term, led Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa just 50% to 47% in a Texas Southern University poll.
In the governor’s race, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D) led Rep. John James (R-Mich.) by six points in a Marist poll.

Kansas hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932. Now, Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) faces the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist megachurch pastor, who held an edge in the final Emerson College poll.

In Iowa, Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) have toggled between leading and trailing all fall for the seat of retiring Sen. Joni Ernst. State Auditor Rob Sand (D) led Republican Zach Lahn in every October poll for governor.

In Nebraska, independent Dan Osborn and Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) were tied at 49% in a YouGov poll. No Democrat is on the ballot. The Omaha-based 2nd District, vacant after Rep. Don Bacon’s (R-Neb.) retirement, leans Democratic.
In Minnesota, Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan led former NFL reporter Michele Tafoya, a Republican, 54% to 40% in a New York Times/Siena poll.

In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley (D) led Rep. Tom Tiffany (R.) 51% to 44% among likely voters in the last Marquette Law School poll. The race is to succeed retiring Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat.
In Arizona, Gov. Katie Hobbs (D) has led Rep. Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.) in polling throughout the fall.

In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) led Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman (R) 54% to 40% in Siena’s final poll. Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) is in a tight race with Democrat Cait Conley in the Hudson Valley’s 17th District.
10 p.m. ET: Polls close in Montana, Nevada and Utah
Montana is home to a close House race in its 1st Congressional District between Republican Aaron Flint and Democrat Sam Forstag.

Republicans are generally favored to win its three-way Senate race as well. Ironically, many Democratic operatives angled to sabotage their nominee, Alani Bankhead, feeling that independent hopeful Seth Bodnar had a better shot at winning. But she refused to bow out of the race.
In Nevada, incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) is facing a brutal reelection fight against the state’s Attorney General Aaron Ford.
11 p.m. ET: Polls close in California, Idaho, Oregon and Washington

If the battle for control of the House winds up being tighter than expected, California could be determinative of the balance of power in the lower chamber. Unfortunately, it’s notoriously slow at counting votes.
That was the case in the 2022 midterm election cycle, where the expected red wave ended up closer than expected, and it took nearly eight days before the party in control of the House was clear.
Oregon is also home to a buzzy gubernatorial race between the unpopular incumbent Gov. Tina Kotek (D) and Republican Sen. Christine Drazan, who put up a spirited fight against her in 2022.
12 a.m. ET: Polls close in Hawaii
The Paradise of the Pacific hasn’t generated a lot of national attention with its midterm races this year, but polls close in the youngest state in the union around 12 am ET.
1 a.m. ET: Polls close in Alaska

As is tradition, Alaska, which is four hours behind, will be the final state to close. The Last Frontier has one of the most fraught Senate races in the country, between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska).
The race has been roiled by a bombshell report that Peltola’s allies recruited Dan J. Sullivan, known as “Decoy Dan,” into the race to confuse voters.
Beyond litigation, Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system that could take time to determine the winner if the election ends up being as close as the polls suggest.
Ahead of Election Day, Alaska’s Division of Elections briefed reporters that the results could begin coming in around 12:45 a.m. ET, according to Scripps News.

articles.headline: Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge
keyFacts: The EU General Court ruled that cloud trade association CISPE can keep the identities of members backing its VMware merger challenge confidential from Broadcom.
CISPE filed an action last year to annul the European Commission's approval of Broadcom's acquisition of VMware without conditions.
CISPE stated that its immediate objective is to have the European Commission's unconditional clearance of the acquisition annulled.
body: Euro cloud trade association CISPE can keep the identities of members backing its VMware merger challenge confidential from Broadcom following a ruling by the EU General Court.
Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe filed an action last year seeking to annul the European Commission's approval of Broadcom's acquisition of the cloud and virtualization giant.

CISPE believes the Commission erred in allowing the purchase to go ahead without imposing any conditions on Broadcom to protect the many European cloud providers and their customers who depend on VMware's software.

Broadcom sought access to redacted information identifying members supporting the action, arguing that it needed the information to challenge the action's admissibility. CISPE says the ruling allows the case to proceed without disclosing those identities to Broadcom.

"It is a procedural ruling on confidentiality rather than a decision on the substance of the case, but it removes the immediate obstacle to the action moving forward," a CISPE spokesperson told The Register .

CISPE argued that identifying the members, which are or have been VMware customers, would expose them to a significant risk of retaliation because of Broadcom's market power. Those members had supplied information about their commercial relationships with VMware.

As far as the case itself goes, CISPE says it warned the Commission that Broadcom would use VMware's pre-eminent position in the private cloud market to rewrite licensing terms and reshape the market in its favor.

Just a month after Broadcom's acquisition concluded in November 2023, partners were informed that VMware's channel program was to end in early 2024, and that Broadcom was also ditching the majority of VMware's Cloud Services Providers , keeping only a select few that had the largest turnover.

Despite Broadcom CEO Hock Tan publicly stating that inflating prices was not his strategy, that is what happened. AT&T says that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent price increase , for example. Meanwhile, nine out of ten respondents to a recent survey of VMware customers said they were considering moving to alternatives.

CISPE, which represents 48 cloud infrastructure service providers across the EU, says fewer than 20 European providers remain authorized to offer VMware-based services, down from more than a thousand.
Commenting on the latest ruling, CISPE Secretary General Francisco Mingorance declared it a good day for the organization and for the rule of law in Europe.

"The case matters even more today than when we filed it. In the three years since the European Commission waved this deal through without conditions, Broadcom has dismantled the European VMware channel ," he said .

"Those excluded have until 31 March, 2027, to sell their infrastructure or their customers to a competitor chosen by Broadcom, or to close. This is the foreclosure the European Commission was warned about."
We asked CISPE what outcome it hoped to achieve, nearly three years after the acquisition closed.

"The immediate objective is to have the Commission's unconditional clearance annulled, on the basis that it failed to properly assess the effect of the acquisition on European cloud providers and the VMware channel," CISPE's spokesperson told The Register .
The Commission did impose conditions concerning interoperability with rival hardware, but CISPE argues these did not address the risks to cloud providers.

"We appreciate that it's a long shot (although there is precedent)," the spokesperson continued. "We have (along with others) also filed a competition complaint with the Directorate-General for Competition against Broadcom for its actions post-merger."

The precedent referred to is the EC approval given to the merger of Sony and BMG's music divisions in 2004, which was ruled to be not of "the requisite legal standard" two years later. The deal was subsequently reassessed and re-cleared.

"Ultimately, we want to do whatever we can to bring Broadcom to the table to negotiate and ideally end some of its most egregious practices so that European cloud providers can once again support cloud customers in a commercially fair and viable manner," the spokesperson added.
The Register asked Broadcom to comment The European Commission declined to comment on procedural matters . ®

articles.headline: What to watch in UEFA Champions League: Michael Carrick's Manchester United future on the line
keyFacts: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick faces mounting pressure as his team prepares for a critical Champions League match against Roma.
Carrick stated that he does not feel his job is in jeopardy and praised the continued commitment of his players.
Inter Milan players and coaches raised concerns about the team's attitude and mentality following recent losses and poor form.
body: The midway point of the Champions League phase is upon us, and already the pressure is beginning to build on some of the biggest clubs in Europe. For some -- the likes of Bayern Munich, Inter and Manchester City -- the coming days will be about scrabbling back up the table and establishing a grip on one of the coveted top eight berths.

Altogether more significant are those teams who might have to legitimately worry about whether they can reach the top 24. On current form Manchester United are certainly among them, and their home game against Roma threatens to be critical for the club's Champions League prospects. Perhaps the future of their manager too.
How long can Carrick last?

A little over a week ago it seemed only logical to log the remainder of Michael Carrick's time as Manchester United manager in hours. Back-to-back defeats to Como and Bournemouth, each by a three-goal margin, had the club hovering around the drop zone in both the Premier League and Champions League standings. Club captain Bruno Fernandes had openly questioned Carrick's tactics, fostering a greater sense of mutiny in the aftermath of center back Lisandro Martinez turning both barrels on those in charge of appointing the manager and signing players.

Remarkably, Carrick endured, part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the rest of the hierarchy concluding that the manager, who had led United to third last season, deserved time to right this listing ship. In many ways, events on Saturday vindicated that assessment. At Stamford Bridge the Red Devils had much the better of the first half, a coiled spring ready to blitz Chelsea on the counter. The only slight problem, one obviously out of Carrick's control, was that they did not put the ball in the net. Then the United midfield whooshed open like the doors of the Starship Enterprise to let Morgan Rogers score the opener, and everything adequate was undone in a 14-minute, Lisandro Martinez-authored head loss.

You can't really hold the manager responsible for that, not when so many coaches have tried and failed to quell United's appetite for self-destruction. Then again, it's not like you can sack the players midway through the season. If the situation gets perilous, there's not much you can do but start afresh in the dugout and hope against reason that Eddie Howe (or whoever else) can get through to this squad in a way his predecessors couldn't.

Right now you'd doubt that Manchester United are on the cusp of existential peril -- relegation to the Championship seems a long shot -- but they are at risk of being a few million worse off from their European campaign. Lose at home to Roma and they would have three points with half the league phase played. Still to play: Sporting and Villarreal away, RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich at home. That makes for a critical occasion against Roma, whose free-scoring attack must have been licking their lips on Saturday lunchtime. This has the makings of a brutal ending to a tenure that started with such promise.

Carrick sees things differently. "Perception is a funny thing," he said on Monday, insisting he does not feel like a coach with two games left to save his job. "You can make things look different ways and think about all sorts of different things. The commitment of the players to the club, to me, to each other - do not question at all. We need to play better, we can make better decisions, but the commitment is not a thing at all."

And yet, much as Carrick's perception of the group might quickly change, so could the game's view of why the United hierarchy stood by its man a week ago. Was the manager afforded faith for the long-term job or did his employers just conclude there was no sense in rushing a change ahead of a tricky three-game run before the international break? Fail to beat Roma and Aston Villa and we will surely find out.
Do Inter need an attitude shift?

Even in the aftermath of a derby defeat on Halloween night, it did not seem there was much cause for doom and gloom among the Inter ranks. A three-point deficit to league leaders Lazio is surely retrievable for the defending champions, and while they have only three points from their first three games, winning a man down against Shakhtar Donetsk eased any lingering sense of crisis about Champions League progression.

And yet the mood music emanating from the blue-and-black half of the San Siro paints a far more worrying picture. Head coach Cristian Chivu questioned the "approach and determination" of his side, senior center back Alessandro Bastoni spoke of an "inadequate" mentality and Nicolo Barella was the most damning of the lot. "We haven't had the right attitude since the start of the season, and it's a negative thing," he said, framing his side's struggles as being against tiredness as much as their opponents.

All of which might be something of an overreaction to Milan scoring three goals from five shots worth 0.57 expected goals in the first half at the weekend. Are there deep-seated problems with Inter or is this a team missing a host of senior players, among them Lautaro Martinez, whose absence at the weekend prompted Chivu to unsuccessfully experiment with Marcus Thuram as a lone striker?

Martinez will be missing for the trip to Feyenoord, but even without the captain, Bastoni, John Stones and Curtis Jones, there is the requisite quality in the Inter ranks to win well in Rotterdam (particularly if Chivu brings Federico Dimarco back into the XI). Whatever their attitude might be, it has not stopped them running up a supremely impressive 2.5 non-penalty expected goals per game. As for Europe, it would not have taken that many bounces going in a different direction for this team to have seven-plus points and be thinking about a return to the last 16. Without wishing to go too Leslie Nielsen about this, there really is nothing to see here.

Equally, when your players and coaches start talking in such apocalyptic terms, it is much more likely to bring on, well, the apocalypse. Or at least its Champions League league phase equivalent of an unseeded berth in the knockout playoffs/punishment round. That and some dropped points against Como and Atalanta.
Can Kane elevate injury-riddled Bayern?

Last time out we suggested that Arsenal's depth might hold the key against Bayern Munich late on and, like the stopped clock this column is, we were vindicated as Viktor Gyokeres turned provider for Declan Rice's late winner. Ultimately in the closing stages all Vincent Kompany had to turn to off the bench to aid his attack was a banged-up Luis Diaz and a faltering youngster in Lennart Karl. A fortnight later, even that would be an upgrade on the situation Bayern find themselves in as they travel to Madrid.

Saturday's 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund came at the cost of Ismael Saibari and Serge Gnabry, both of whom will be missing for some time yet. Jamal Musiala is also on the sidelines with a thigh injury and Diaz has only just returned to the field as he steps up his recovery from a hamstring injury. The best-case scenario for Bayern is that Michael Olise, who also exited early at the weekend, is able to play in some capacity, but director of sport Max Eberl described the Frenchman's situation as "day to day".

If Olise is not fit, it may be that the three attacking midfielders are Karl and two left backs, Alphonso Davies and Nathan Brown. It would take quite the center forward to knit all that together. A Ballon d'Or winner. Harry Kane's headline contribution to Der Klassiker might have been the missed penalty at 1-0, but the No. 9 ended this game with an assist for Dayot Upamecano and 0.43 expected assists total. Remarkably for a center forward, that was not even that far ahead of his season average of 0.32. That's 97th percentile for creation. It will not surprise you to know he ranks in the 99th percentile for shots and xG.

As Arsenal discovered to their cost in the last round of Champions League games, you can take away Kane's shooting chances, you can even take away his elite supporting cast, but he might still find a way to lay one on a plate for a teammate.

articles.headline: Apple will start mandating age requirements for dating apps
keyFacts: Apple is adding new content descriptor questions to App Store Connect to ensure accurate age ratings for dating and location-sharing apps.
Apps involving dating between real people or virtual companions will receive a mandatory minimum age rating of 18 plus.
Developers must answer the new questionnaire items by January 12, 2027, for all existing and new applications.
body: Apple will start mandating age requirements for dating apps
They will apply to apps that allow AI companion relationships, as well.

Apple will start asking developers more questions about their apps to help the company ensure that their age ratings accurately reflect their content. Specifically, it will add new content descriptor questions to App Store Connect, the company's web-based management platform for developers. One of the new descriptors will require them to declare whether their app shares the real-world location of the user with another person or group. The other one will require them to disclose whether their app has features, which enable dating "between real people and/or a virtual companion that engages a user in sexual or romantic content."

All apps declared to have dating and relationship content will get a minimum age rating of 18+. That means they will not appear in the App Store for kids under 18 if their parents or guardians have set app content restrictions on their device. If underage users who can see them on the store try to purchase or download them, they will be required to provide Apple proof that they're adult. As for apps that share location, they will not be affected by age ratings in most regions. Some countries do have rules for apps like that, however, like Brazil that requires apps that share locations to have an age rating of 16-years-old and up.

The new content descriptors will show up in the management platform on November 16. Developers will have to answer both inquiries in the age rating questionnaire when submitting a new app or making changes to an existing one. By January 12, 2027, they must have already answered both questions for all their applications.

articles.headline: DOJ faces ‘heavy lift’ in Alaska election appeal as separate criminal probe continues
keyFacts: Legal experts said the Justice Department faces an uphill battle and tight timeline to overturn a judge's dismissal of its Alaska Senate election lawsuit before voting ends Tuesday.

The Justice Department appealed after U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the lawsuit over standing, ruling federal officials failed to show how their remedy would prevent voter confusion without compromising ballot secrecy.
Legal experts noted that a failed appeal or a civil defeat would not necessarily affect a separate ongoing criminal investigation into the recruitment of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan.
body: The Justice Department faces an uphill legal battle in its bid to overturn a federal judge's dismissal of its Alaska Senate election lawsuit, according to legal experts who questioned whether the government can secure meaningful relief before voting ends Tuesday — even as a separate criminal investigation continues.

DOJ filed a notice of appeal after Obama-appointed U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed its lawsuit Sunday over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot. The judge ruled that federal officials lacked standing because they had not demonstrated how their proposed remedy could address potential voter confusion without compromising ballot secrecy.

With voting ending Tuesday, attorneys told Fox News Digital that even a successful appeal could leave the government scrambling to obtain an injunction or return to district court, while a defeat would leave the civil case dismissed without necessarily affecting potential criminal charges arising from the alleged recruitment of the second Sullivan.
DOJ SET TO APPEAL RULING IN ALASKA SENATE RACE DISPUTE OVER ‘DECOY DAN’

"The federal judge dismissed on a procedural issue — standing," election attorney Jason Torchinsky of Virginia-based firm Holtzman Vogel told Fox News Digital. "So if the government were to prevail, it would either have to seek injunctive relief from the appeals court in the first instance, a very high bar, or go back down to the district court to seek relief."
"Given the time available between now and close of polls [Tuesday], this is a heavy lift for the government," Torchinsky added.
A reversal would not automatically change Alaska's election results. DOJ would still need to obtain specific judicial relief, potentially requiring further proceedings in district court.
Former federal prosecutor and ex-Pentagon official Cully Stimson similarly said that DOJ will have difficulty securing any immediate relief in its effort to pause the Sullivan-Peltola contest.
While Gleason was appointed by Obama, Stimson suggested the ruling did not appear partisan and said uncertainty remains because voting had not yet concluded.
"I'm not surprised that the judge did this. I don't think it would matter whether an Obama judge or any other judge appointed by any other president," Stimson told Fox News Digital.
"Asking for injunctive relief way before anything even happens is a reach," he said, adding Alaska falls under the San Francisco-based Ninth Circuit , which will hear any appeal.

But Stimson suggested DOJ may have a longer-term objective beyond winning an immediate injunction: establishing a legal record that could support further proceedings after the election, once the votes are counted.
TRUMP PROSECUTIONS UNDER BIDEN SET PRECEDENT FOR DOJ’S ALASKA ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE, EX-FEC CHAIR SAYS

"They may be filing these suits to establish a record and force Alaska and others supporting the status quo to defend what's happening, knowing that there's some level of confusion, and they have the legal wheels churning," he said. "So after the vote is [over], they've started the legal wheels rolling."
Former Assistant U.S. Attorney for North Florida Zack Smith added that if the Ninth Circuit does not hear the case promptly, DOJ could seek emergency review from the U.S. Supreme Court.
While the Alaska case is considered unprecedented, according to the experts, the idea of a Supreme Court expedition at election time is not.

On Dec. 9, 2000, one day after the Florida Supreme Court ordered a manual recount of disputed ballots in the Bush v. Gore presidential election dispute involving "hanging chads," then-Texas Gov. George W. Bush’s legal team successfully sought emergency intervention.
The court ultimately decided in Bush’s favor within a week.

Since the disputed 2000 election, which featured "hanging chads" on hole-punched paper ballots and the Brooks Brothers Riot at the Miami-Dade elections office, DOJ has become well-accustomed to the expedited-review process , the experts said.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP DOJ'S THREATS AGAINST ELECTION WORKERS AHEAD OF 2026 MIDTERMS
"DOJ is familiar with kind of working quickly, getting things to the Supreme Court, and so I wouldn't be completely surprised if you were to see something like that," Smith said.
Bush v. Gore offers a procedural parallel because federal courts were asked to intervene in the administration of a state-run election.

"Florida was conducting the election in the manner under Florida law, under this time, place and manners set out by Florida law even though it was a federal election," Stimson said. "They used a particular type of ballot, which had those so-called dangling chads, which were punch-holes that didn't come the whole way off, so the hole was left with a little tag, essentially like a skin tag, and eventually the Supreme Court of Florida ruled."

"But because there were federal violations, eventually the Supreme Court weighed in and stopped it. And at no point in time had the vice president’s (Albert Gore) vote count ever surpassed that of the governor (Bush) and because it was a federal interest, the Supreme Court stepped in and stopped this counting at the state level."
Alex Charns, an attorney who has argued in federal court, told Fox News Digital that the clock has run out and DOJ's goal of segregating ballots based on voter intent is no longer possible.

"I've litigated against the USDOJ for over thirteen years in federal court. I've practiced law in Durham, N.C., for 43 years. The USDOJ filed a case without legal merit and its appeal is likely to fail," he said.

"In addition, voting ends [Tuesday]. The relief they seek isn't possible — ballots already cast can't be segregated. Also, one cannot tell why any voter voted in a particular way. The appeal is unlikely to be successful."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

In a statement from the DOJ's "Rapid Response" (DOJ-RR) office, a spokesperson said the court "dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters."
"Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes," DOJ-RR said, announcing their appeal.

Stimson cautioned that the outcome of the civil litigation would have little bearing on the separate criminal investigation, which could uncover evidence supporting additional legal action even if DOJ's appeal fails.

"As long as that criminal investigation is going on, you're not breathing easy," he said, adding that evidence uncovered by federal investigators could potentially provide grounds for a separate civil lawsuit.

articles.headline: West Ham turn to Scott Parker after sacking Nuno Espírito Santo as head coach
keyFacts: West Ham sacked head coach Nuno Espírito Santo following a 3-1 defeat by West Bromwich Albion that left the team eighth in the Championship.
West Ham are poised to appoint Scott Parker as his successor, with optimism he will take charge for the upcoming match against Cardiff City.
The club board stated that a change was necessary to keep their objectives and promotion expectations on track after a thorough review.
body: West Ham are poised to appoint Scott Parker as their manager after sacking Nuno Espírito Santo. Parker has been out of work since leaving Burnley last season but there is optimism he will be in place when West Ham visit Cardiff City on Wednesday.

The club kept faith with Nuno after their relegation from the Premier League last season but patience has snapped with the side eighth in the Championship after the 3-1 defeat by West Bromwich Albion last Saturday.

Nuno struggled to get his ideas across after taking over from Graham Potter in September 2025. He had 33 games to save West Ham from relegation but his tactics were poor, his team selections were confusing and his signings have not worked out.

West Ham are intent on an instant return to the top flight and want to get their automatic promotion hopes back on track. Parker is a former West Ham player and his backroom staff is expected to include his former teammate Mark Noble.

“Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club’s objectives and expectations remain on track,” a club statement said.

“Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also departed. West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future.”

articles.headline: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe’s startup scene
keyFacts: Yvonne Bajela announced that her new venture capital fund, Evertrue, closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I on Tuesday.
Evertrue will focus on early-stage investments across the U.K. and Europe, primarily targeting AI and fintech sectors.
The fund plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years with average checks around £350,000.
body: Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmellow, and robotaxi Mooves.
On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue, officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I.

“After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.”

The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.”

As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said.

However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025.

Still Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.”

Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it pour £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size.

“Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.”

Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S.

Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.”
“I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued.

She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mistusi and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.”
“I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.”
