Reeves and engineering genius Dana Starr travel into the Badlands to find a missing scientist connected to Reeves' past.
body: Spoilers follow for Bass X Machina Episode 1, “Until Then... I'm Bass Reeves.” The full six-episode season is available now on Netflix.

The latest animated production from Studio Mir (Devil May Cry, X-Men '97, My Adventures With Superman, etc.) to make its way to our airwaves… or streaming waves – whatever we’re calling them these days – Bass X Machina is, based on this first episode, a fun and violent excursion into the world of the steampunk Western, but with an eye to Black history. Or rather, alt-history, since this series gives us a Wild West where robots and cyborgs are the norm, even while the face-in-the-dirt killin’ remains as ruthless as ever.

Brian Tyree Henry, who also is an executive producer on the series, voices Bass Reeves, or this world’s version of Bass Reeves, who of course in reality was a historic lawman; an ex-slave who went on to become a Deputy U.S. Marshal, Reeves has been portrayed in movies, TV and elsewhere many times over the years, perhaps most notably in recent years in Damon Lindelof’s Watchmen (where his legend inspired that world’s first superhero, Hooded Justice ).

As the first episode starts, Reeves explains in VO how, after the Civil War, the Union Army was “saddled with thousands of Black soldiers they didn’t know what to do with. And after having known the horrors of war, some of these soldiers didn’t know what to do with themselves.” Some chose the life of the gun in the West, some became Buffalo Soldiers, and “some legendary few… became lawmen.”

Only when we first meet Reeves, he’s a bounty hunter, not a lawman – a fact which is driven home immediately when he shoots two opponents without thinking twice about it. In fact, he’s also part machine, utilizing a steam-powered arm which has replaced his real appendage at some point in his violent history. Quick flashbacks/dreams to some blood-red past event indicate we’ll eventually learn the story of how he came by that arm, but not today.

The action in this first episode is fun and bloody, with a dynamic range of camera moves and angles as Reeves, for starters, shoots the heck out of a gang of crooks. The action in this first episode is fun and bloody, with a dynamic range of camera moves and angles as Reeves, for starters, shoots the heck out of a gang of crooks during a train heist. Bullets enter (and exit) foreheads with style, while the speed of the racing train and pyrotechnics of a Gatling gun add to the overall excitement of the opening scene. Henry’s Reeves also establishes his general apathy towards his opponents right out of the gate, such as when, after dispatching one fellow’s two brothers, the man cries, “You took my brothers away!” Henry’s Reeves dispassionately responds, “You’re back with ‘em now” before finishing the guy off with a single shot. Dang.

After an opening credits sequence that further hints at Reeves’ origin story, complete with propulsive theme song by Janelle Monáe, the series’ main storyline is established. A scientist named Dr. Eugene Starr has gone missing, apparently into the Native American territory called the Badlands. But not just any scientist: It seems Starr, or someone close to him, has been experimenting on the “magic metal that’s going around” – and using it on people. Whether or not this magic metal is the same substance that has made “boilertech” commonplace in this world is unclear, but regardless, human experimentation is clearly a topic of interest for Reeves, who says that his arm “wasn’t lost. It was stolen.”

Tati Gabrielle voices Dana Starr, a young woman who is the niece of the missing scientist and an engineering genius who winds up playing sidekick to Reeves. She’s able to build handy gadgets while also calculating things like, say, how much time Dr. Starr has left to live after the possibility of “predation, murder, dysentery, despair.” (The answer is three days.) Monáe also voices Reeves’ wife Glory, and we learn that the couple have two sons as well. But Reeves can’t rest – or be a father and husband – while he knows that the key to his past could be lurking out there with Dr. Starr…

Created by LeSean Thomas, who’s also worked on series like Yasuke, Cannon Busters, and Black Dynamite, Bass X Machina finds a nice balance between the Western tropes, retro-sci-fi tech, bloody violence, and animated style. By the time Episode 1 winds down and Reeves and Dana are heading off into the Badlands to begin their journey – one on a horse and the other on a makeshift boilertech scooter – it’s clear that this has not just been the beginning of a beautiful friendship, but also of a cool new animated world.

articles.headline: U.S. military carries out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island
keyFacts: The U.S. military carried out limited defensive strikes Monday on Iran's Qeshm Island in response to Iranian targeting of U.S. aircraft, according to U.S. officials.
Iranian state media reported five explosions on the island, while Vice President JD Vance expressed optimism about a potential negotiated settlement with Iran.
President Donald Trump stated that Iran wants a settlement and that the strikes are not a resumption of major combat operations.
body: The U.S. military carried out limited strikes Monday on Iran’s Qeshm Island, according to two U.S. officials.

The officials said the U.S. attacks, which came on the eve of crucial U.S. midterm elections and as the Middle East is anxious about the possibility of a return to all-out war, were not a resumption of major combat operations in Iran. They described the attacks as self-defense in response to Iran’s ongoing efforts to target maritime shipping and U.S. assets.
The U.S. continues to intercept drones and missiles that are targeting shipping every day, one of the U.S. officials said.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has routinely targeted and shot at U.S. manned and unmanned aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz and in the area over the past few weeks, one of the U.S. officials said.
The U.S. is occasionally striking Iranian missile launchers in self-defense when the Revolutionary Guard shoots at U.S. aircraft, the official said.
Iran tried to target a U.S. aircraft again, leading to the U.S. strike on Qeshm to take out the launcher, the official said, calling it part of ongoing operations.
A third U.S. official said, “This was a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets.”
Iranian state media reported that five explosions were heard Monday on Qeshm Island.
President Donald Trump had said the U.S. would not launch strikes on Iran before Tuesday’s midterm elections.
The unpopular Iran war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.

The administration was last known to have carried out some attacks in early September, but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from getting to the global market. A third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East.

Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal can still be struck to prevent Trump from following through on his threat to potentially order new strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.

Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, few details of which have been offered by the White House. Trump told reporters the letter was focused on assisting Iran with “medical supplies and various things.”
Vance suggested Monday that there was reason to believe the U.S. and Iran could still come to an agreement.

“We’ve had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” he told reporters when he was asked about the letter, adding that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We’re going to keep on working at it.”

The region remains on edge about the prospect of the U.S.’ resuming full-scale operations against Iran. The back-channel efforts are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way forward in the eight-month-old war, which has rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed for renewed strikes even before the Israeli election last week as he sought to highlight his security credentials to a public deeply scarred by the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks.
But the war has also loomed large for American voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Oil prices dropped sharply Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war appeared to show signs of progress.

Trump noted the drop Monday in a speech in Washington, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion.
“I don’t know if you even call it a war, because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said. Earlier he posted on Truth Social that “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible.”
He has frequently asserted that the two sides are close to a deal to end the conflict, though one has so far failed to materialize.
Iran has repeatedly said it is open to a diplomatic resolution, but has largely stuck to its demands.

Tehran “has delivered a firm and rational response to the American side and the ball is now in America’s court to prevent a war,” Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tuesday.

articles.headline: Starbucks Drive-Thru AI Could Know What You Want Before You Do
keyFacts: Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol announced that the company will test drive-thru artificial intelligence in fiscal year 2027 to recognize customers and take orders.
The planned AI integration aims to make drive-up ordering faster and more personal, though methods like facial recognition or license plate reading remain unspecified.
Experts and union representatives raised concerns about potential privacy violations, technical errors, and the impact on workers amid ongoing labor disputes.
body: Could an AI barista know you’re craving an iced caramel macchiato? Starbucks says it will begin testing artificial intelligence for drive-up ordering — including recognizing customers as they approach — as the company focuses on integrating more automated tech, CEO Brian Niccol said on last week’s fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call.

The idea is to make ordering “faster, more convenient and more personal” for drive-up customers, which account for roughly half of all Starbucks patrons, according to Niccol. The company would begin testing background AI models for drive-thrus sometime during fiscal year 2027, which ends Sept. 28, 2027. There were no specifics as to where the testing would take place or how it would affect food and drink prices.
Niccol said AI would help input orders “more accurately and efficiently” while the baristas talk to drive-up customers to increase personal connection and speed up service.
More from CNET

The AI could also know what you want, or might want, before you even engage with the human barista. Niccol said the company is exploring ways for automated systems to recognize repeat customers as they drive up and offer “personalized digital menus,” possibly including suggested purchases.

While the exact kind of systems that would be tested to recognize customers weren’t specified, possible methods could include facial recognition, license plate reading or perhaps mobile app detection. It also remains to be seen which methods would require explicit customer consent or offer an opt-out mechanism. In an email to CNET, a Starbucks representative did not confirm which specific technology would be employed.

The representative said that Starbucks is already using AI in its operations through Green Dot Assist, which helps workers look up drink recipes, troubleshoot equipment issues and coordinate staffing. The company also uses Smart Queue to figure out sequencing of orders that come in via in-store, drive-thru, mobile app or delivery.
Do customers even want more AI?

Several major fast-food chains are using or testing AI to process drive-thru orders, including McDonald’s, Taco Bell, KFC, White Castle and Wendy’s. Customer reviews have been mixed so far, with the main problems being botched orders, lengthy processing and the inability of bots to answer questions, according to customer research from restaurant tech website Canopy.

Burger King, meanwhile, decided to pull back on using AI for drive-thru because some customers drove off rather than place their orders with a bot. The company is still testing AI but said it wants to give people the option of ordering from a human.

It’s unclear what Starbucks’ goal is or what customers the company is trying to appeal to, said Uttara M. Ananthakrishnan, AI researcher and associate professor at the University of Washington. But there’s plenty to be skeptical about.

“AI in face-to-face customer service will fail in many edge cases and has many potential PR problems with no clear benefits,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET. “It is better to defer until there is a broader general acceptance among the public.”

Ananthakrishnan said one flaw of using bots is voice recognition — many AI models are trained on general US accents and don’t perform well with non-native speakers or international accents. Surrounding noise from vehicles and weather can also affect how well the bot understands the customer through a kiosk microphone. That could pose health risks, Ananthakrishnan said, if, for example, someone is allergic to nuts and the AI misinterprets the request as “no nuts.”

McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru experiment with IBM in 2024, when bots were unable to understand various accents and dialects. The fast-food giant recently launched a new experiment with AI bot Archy as part of an $8.5 billion modernization plan. There was also a fake order that went viral when someone ordered 18,000 waters at a Taco Bell, and the AI processed it.

Most of Ananthakrishnan’s students have said they don’t want to talk to AI during their customer service interactions. However, more people might accept drive-thru AI if they know that mistakes will be rectified quickly, Ananthakrishnan said.

In a Bluesky post by More Perfect Union, an Emmy-winning nonprofit newsroom that advocates for workers, the reaction to Starbucks’ AI plan was overwhelmingly negative, with commenters complaining about privacy violations and pointing to the potential for “dynamic pricing” based on customer behavior and algorithms

Starbucks has said it doesn’t use surveillance pricing, a discriminatory method that’s been increasingly used by hotels, airlines and retailers. Still, a 2025 report in The Washington Post indicated that loyal customers using the Starbucks app more often might be getting fewer promotional deals.
More AI, fewer workers?

In a 2026 statement on the use of AI, the company says: “Our business is rooted in human connection — and our technology is designed to strengthen it, not replace it.” But Starbucks’ human connection with its workers has been problematic, and AI isn’t known for improving labor relations.

Since initiating a major organizing blitz starting in late 2021, Starbucks employees have formed unions at nearly 700 stores in the US, demanding higher pay and more robust staffing levels. Workers say they are not given enough hours so the company can avoid providing benefits, and are often given very short notice about shift changes. Last year, the NLRB said Starbucks “engaged in a scorched earth campaign and pattern of misconduct in response to union organizing.”

Since taking over as CEO in September 2024, Niccol has cut more than 2,000 employees as part of his Back to Starbucks strategy, which has resulted in simplified menus, reduced wait times and the closure of some shops.

In August, Starbucks Workers United, which represents 12,000 baristas, announced an open-ended national consumer boycott against corporate-owned Starbucks locations. The call accused the company of violating US labor law and attempting to break up the union, while also criticizing the corporate push for AI. “Starbucks has repeatedly demonstrated a lack of care for the workers who fuel the company’s profits by wasting millions of dollars on AI and technology that doesn’t work, launching countless gimmicky drinks designed to distract from real problems, and inventing pointless policies that do nothing but make workers’ jobs harder,” the call read.

In a 2025 interview with Current Affairs, union organizer Jason Woods said the company was trying to use AI to place orders but couldn’t handle staffing when an employee calls out. “They want to use algorithms to deploy our plays,” he said. “It’s inhumane. It’s anti-worker, anti-labor.”
Starbucks Workers United didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.headline: Epic Just Saved Fortnite–For Now, Anyway
keyFacts: Epic's new One Piece-themed Treasure Hunters season for Fortnite caused player counts to surge significantly over the weekend.
The publisher attracted players by offering free item-shop cosmetics in treasure chests and rebalancing gameplay mechanics.
Epic aims to retain these players despite the upcoming release of GTA VI.
body: It's been a rough year for Fortnite , but Epic took a big swing with its new One Piece-themed Treasure Hunters season and, thankfully, it's paying off. Player counts are way up, with Fortnite's main Battle Royale mode averaging four times as many players on Sunday for the season launch than it had been the past few months. The numbers then got even larger on Monday, somehow. Fortnite BR now looks on track to have its best month since the original Fortnite OG mini-season in 2023. With GTA VI on the horizon, that's very good news for Epic.

There is one particularly obvious reason why the numbers are spiking so hard: The Treasure Hunt is giving players the chance to win two weeks of free item-shop cosmetics every time they open a treasure chest. But Epic has also made a few major changes to BR that make it more fun to play than it has been at any previous point during Chapter 7. The hunt for free cosmetics might be the thing that got everyone's attention, but the other changes might actually get some of these new and returning folks to stick around into Chapter 8.
Let's take a look at what Epic did right by ending Chapter 7 with this new mini-season.
Treasure Hunt

I've complained before about the sort of transparently coercive engagement mechanics that Epic has been using in Chapter 7, but I'd say they found a genuinely excellent one with the Treasure Hunt. Any time you or one of your squadmates opens a treasure chest, you have a chance of winning one of several free cosmetics, including an A$AP Rocky skin and a Mercedes SUV. But there's also kind of a Willy Wonka golden ticket that a lucky few will find, which allows them to claim everything in the item shop for free for two weeks.

That's an engagement technique I can get behind, because winning free cosmetics is the sort of thing that appeals broadly to the vast majority of Fortnite players, and the entry fee is just to play the game the same way you usually would. It's not something you can grind out, so there's nothing to stress about--you just play, and maybe get lucky.
Sprites are no longer gameplay critical

It was smart of Epic to introduce the Sprite-collecting mechanic in Season 3, but the problem was that they were essential to gameplay. If you didn't engage with that mechanic, you would be at a disadvantage in fights. During Season 4, for example, if you didn't have a Sonic or a Jackrabbit sprite late in a sweaty match, you were probably gonna end up getting cooked by somebody who did. Using the sprites never felt optional.

Sprites have returned once again during Treasure Hunters season, but their abilities are no longer the sort of thing that significantly changes the balance of a fight. This season, you aren't going to lose a lot of matches because the other guy has a maxed-out Sonic sprite and can run twice as fast as you. It's the perfect balance: The folks who like sprites can keep collecting them, and the rest of us can do whatever we want.
It feels like Fortnite again

I don't think Chapter 7 has been particularly bad compared with previous chapters, but it introduced a lot of fundamental changes that have made it feel strange for Fortnite old timers, like the rearranged UI, buyable reboot cards, and a faster time-to-kill that has made BR much more unforgiving.

But Treasure Hunters season has rebalanced the gameplay to make BR feel more like it used to. The loot pool doesn't include any weapons that that your average player is going to laser you with from a distance, making it easier to react to and survive ambushes. The removal of buyable reboot cards means squads are more likely to commit to a fight than run away at the first sign of trouble.

And it's been quite a while since we had new anime Mythics that are as fun as the new One Piece abilities, particularly Ace's fire powers, which come from the Flame-Flame Fruit. If you're the type of Fortnite player who pines for the days of Deku's Smash (all the way back in Chapter 4) like I am, you'll have an absolute blast with the Flame-Flame Fruit. And don't even get me started on Zoro's Three Swords, which is Fortnite's most interesting and amusing new melee weapon since the ODM Gear from Attack on Titan in Chapter 4.

Coming off Chapter 7 Season 4, which I found to be actively irritating up until Fortnitemares began in October, this Treasure Hunters mini-season already feels like a breath of fresh air. Even if we didn't have this hunt for free cosmetics and Tim Sweeney's golden ticket to the item shop, this would be a great season of Fortnite.

They've pulled a lot of folks back in with this Treasure Hunt, but it won't be easy to retain them with the release of GTA VI in a few weeks. If Fortnite played the same way it did last season, with the faster TTK and obligatory sprite gameplay, I doubt this surge in players would last long. But I think Epic has given itself a real shot to hold onto at least some of our attention with the changes it's made.

articles.headline: "At Home in Space" opens, caps Air and Space Museum renovation
keyFacts: The Smithsonian completed a seven-year, nearly $1 billion renovation of the National Air and Space Museum's flagship building in Washington, DC.
The museum debuted its final spaceflight exhibition called At Home in Space, which focuses on long-duration spaceflight and living on the International Space Station.
Curator Jennifer Levasseur said the gallery tells the story of human spaceflight progress and sets up future steps like bases on the Moon and Mars.
body: After seven years of work and nearly $1 billion, the Smithsonian has completed the renovation of the National Air and Space Museum’s flagship building in Washington, DC.
On October 30, the museum debuted its last-to-open spaceflight exhibition, returning “home” with a gallery devoted to establishing a spacefaring civilization.

“Welcome to ‘At Home in Space’!” said curator Jennifer Levasseur, who guided us through a virtual tour of the gallery. “This is the story of long-duration spaceflight in the last few decades. We generally call it ‘reaching orbit.’”

“It’s the prep story, the space shuttle story. It’s what allows us to end up at a place where we have 25-plus years of long-duration spaceflight experience, the capacity for humans to be living in space on the International Space Station (ISS), and then it carries that story forward. So the middle of our story then becomes the ISS, and the end of the story are the next steps,” said Levasseur.
Entering “At Home”

Over the past several years, the National Air and Space Museum has introduced new galleries showcasing how US astronauts first entered space and landed on the Moon (“Destination Moon”); how robotic probes have explored every planet in our solar system (“Kenneth C. Griffin Exploring the Planets”); how technologies and infrastructure impact our daily lives (“RTX Living in the Space Age Hall”) and what approaches spaceflight will take in the years to come (“Futures in Space”).

“At Home in Space,” which follows the similarly themed “Moving Beyond Earth,” immerses guests in the equipment, spacecraft, and orbital platforms that have enabled humanity from simply visiting space to living there, setting up the near future for bases on the Moon and Mars.

articles.headline: Apple is ‘not able to predict’ when it’ll have enough iPhone Duos to go around
keyFacts: Apple CEO John Ternus stated that the company cannot predict when iPhone Duo supply constraints will end due to high demand and unprecedented memory costs.
Apple launched its first foldable phone for $1,999 last month, which quickly sold out and faced reports of a small percentage of cracked screens.
Ternus reported record-breaking fourth-quarter iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion despite supply chain challenges and higher memory costs.
body: Apple CEO John Ternus doesn’t have a timeline for when iPhone Duo supply constraints could lift. During an interview with Reuters, Ternus said the company is “working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we’re not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.”
Apple is ‘not able to predict’ when it’ll have enough iPhone Duos to go around
John Ternus says Apple is seeing ‘unprecedented’ memory pricing.

Apple launched its first foldable last month for $1,999, featuring a 5.4 outer display and 7.6-inch inner screen. Preorders for the iPhone Duo quickly sold out, with some shipments expected to arrive in 2027. Apple also made a limited number of iPhone Duo models available in-store at launch.
In his interview with Reuters, Ternus also addressed reports about cracked screens, saying “a very small percentage” of iPhone Duos were returned for this issue, and that Apple is replacing them.

The company has contended with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs for months now. This resulted in price increases across its product lineup, along with higher iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max starting prices. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” Ternus said during Apple’s Q4 2026 earnings call on Monday. Ternus added that the company expects to see “even higher memory costs” during Apple’s December quarter but notes that this is “partly offset” by recent price increases.
Even without a standard iPhone 18 model, Apple reported record-breaking iPhone revenue at $57.58 billion during its fourth quarter.
